This is the amyloidogenic core of the peptide, not an inert epitope. Consistent with that, it is the only one of the 25 candidates with a positive GRAVY score (+0.26; every other candidate is between -0.30 and -1.12), which is the computational signature of its aggregation propensity. The platform proposes it as a systemically administered agent to a basal-forebrain target in an explicitly Alzheimer's-framed program and asserts "Fibril Blockade: 100%". There is no aggregation-propensity assessment, no thioflavin-T or seeding assay, no solubility or formulation statement, no immunogenicity assessment (only the unsupported label "Immunogenicity: Low" elsewhere in the file), and no consideration of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities.
findings.why_it_matters: Administering the amyloidogenic core of Abeta to a patient with cerebral amyloid pathology inverts the intended pharmacology: the KLVFF motif is the recognition element by which Abeta monomers self-associate, so an exogenous Abeta(16-35) peptide is a candidate seed and cross-seeder, not a self-evident inhibitor. Short KLVFF-based beta-sheet breakers exist in the literature, but they are deliberately truncated and chemically modified (N-methylated, D-amino-acid, or C-terminally disrupted) precisely to abolish self-assembly; extending to residue 35 restores the full nucleating unit. Separately and independently of any in-vivo seeding question, this is a formulation dead end: a 35-mer with a positive GRAVY and the Abeta hydrophobic core will aggregate in the vial, which is why the absence of any solubility/stability statement matters. And aggregated peptide is the single strongest driver of anti-drug-antibody formation, which the "Immunogenicity: Low" labels elsewhere in the file assert away without data. A reader seeing "Fibril Blockade: 100%" alongside "Seizure Index: 0.01" will conclude the safety case is closed on a molecule whose principal hazard has not been examined.
findings.ground_truth: Abeta(16-35) contains both the central hydrophobic cluster KLVFF (Abeta 16-20) and the C-terminal hydrophobic region, and is the canonical self-assembly-competent fragment; verified here by exact string match against UniProt P05067 residues 687-706 (Abeta 16-35). Correct practice for a beta-sheet-breaker design is to take the minimal recognition motif (typically KLVFF or LPFFD-type analogues), abolish its own aggregation competence by backbone N-methylation, D-amino-acid substitution or proline insertion, and then demonstrate absence of self-aggregation and absence of seeding before any in-vivo claim. Required assays: thioflavin-T kinetics for self-aggregation and for seeding of wild-type Abeta42; size-exclusion and dynamic light scattering for oligomer content in the formulated drug product; and, given the class, an explicit ARIA risk statement.
findings.required_fix: Truncate the fragment to the minimal recognition motif and chemically block self-assembly (N-methylation of the KLVFF backbone or D-residue substitution), or remove the candidate. In either case: delete the "Fibril Blockade: 100%" string at app.js:281 -- it is an unmeasured absolute; add an aggregation-propensity computation (e.g. a TANGO/AGGRESCAN-style or Waltz-style predictor) to every card and flag this candidate explicitly; add explicit fields for predicted solubility, oligomer content and immunogenicity risk with "NOT ASSESSED" where no data exists; and add a prominent note wherever this candidate appears (app.js:277 and app.js:129) stating that the sequence is Abeta(16-35) verbatim and that seeding and cross-seeding must be excluded experimentally before any therapeutic framing.

findings.title: Brain-region-specific targeting is asserted for all 25 candidates with no targeting mechanism, and is provably arbitrary: four pairs of byte-identical sequences are assigned to different brain regions with different Kd and different pLDDT
findings.evidence_location: app.js:153 vs app.js:247 (identical 36-mer KWWKFLRRFWRRLKKYFEELWKKLAEKYFELLKKYG); app.js:173 vs app.js:371 (identical 31-mer CKCHGMSGSCSTKTCWWGBLCPFRRACPDCH); app.js:195 vs app.js:319 (identical 41-mer SEAEFRLFRDVWANYCACYPGWLGCDERACPRCHGFWREVC); app.js:205 vs app.js:361 (identical 37-mer VRACPTGKCEGLRGYTCRCEPGWKGPDCRERACPDCH); corresponding conflicting metadata at app.js:145/146 vs 249/250, 175/176 vs 373/374, 197/198 vs 321/322, 207/208 vs 363/364; README.md:43-92 (the five-region pipeline); README.md:54-56 (region map claiming distinct drug families per region)
findings.what_is_wrong: The platform's organizing claim is that 25 molecules are targeted to five distinct brain regions and cell types, five per region. I extracted all 25 sequences programmatically and found four pairs that are byte-identical yet carry contradictory downstream metadata. Pair 1: the same 36-mer is HippoAChE-AlkaPept-X2 with "Kd = 2.1 nM | AF3 pLDDT = 94.8" targeted to "Hippocampus (CA1 Cholinergic Terminals & Synaptic Cleft)", and simultaneously BasalAChE-GorgeBlock-B1 with "Kd = 0.65 nM | AF3 pLDDT = 94.3" targeted to "Basal Forebrain (Nucleus Basalis of Meynert NBM)" -- a 3.2-fold Kd difference and a different pLDDT for a structure prediction on an identical input string, which is not possible for a deterministic model. Pair 2: the same 31-mer is both a Frizzled-8 agonist in the dentate gyrus SGZ (Kd 1.2 nM, pLDDT 95.1) and a ZO-1 tight-junction protector at the BBB endothelium (Kd 2.8 nM, pLDDT 93.8). Pair 3: the same 41-mer is both an alpha7 nAChR PAM in PFC layer III/V (Kd 1.8 nM) and a TLR4/MD-2 antagonist on microglia (Kd 3.8 nM). Pair 4: the same 37-mer is both a TrkB ERK enhancer in PFC layer V (Kd 0.85 nM) and an astrocytic EAAT2 upregulator (Kd 3.6 nM). Separately, no candidate carries any element capable of producing regional or cell-type selectivity within brain parenchyma -- no cell-type-restricted receptor ligand, no capsid, no promoter, no locally activated prodrug.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the finding that most directly undermines the platform's headline. "25 therapeutics across 5 brain regions" reduces to at most 21 distinct sequences, four of which have been duplicated and relabelled, with the affinity and confidence numbers adjusted to fit the new label. Since affinity and pLDDT are functions of the molecule and its target, and the molecule is identical, at least one number in each pair must be fabricated -- and because the pLDDT differs too, the numbers cannot both come from the same prediction run. More fundamentally for delivery: even if every molecule crossed the BBB perfectly, regional selectivity within parenchyma does not arise from the peptide sequence alone. A soluble peptide entering brain interstitial fluid distributes by diffusion and bulk flow; it goes where the vasculature and the ISF take it, modulated only by target-mediated binding. Claiming that one molecule is a hippocampal CA1 drug and the byte-identical molecule is a nucleus basalis drug asserts a spatial selectivity that no mechanism in the design can deliver. Anyone using this platform to plan a target-engagement or biodistribution study would design the wrong study.
findings.ground_truth: Regional and cell-type selectivity in CNS therapeutics comes from one of a small number of real mechanisms, none of which is present here: (i) a cell-type-restricted receptor with genuinely restricted expression, verified by proteomics rather than asserted; (ii) a delivery vector with intrinsic tropism -- for example the TfR1-retargeted AAV capsid BI-hTFR1, which gave CNS-specific enhanced tropism 40-50x over AAV9 in human-TfR1 knockin mice and no enhancement in wild-type mice (Huang et al., Science 2024;384:1220-1227, PMID 38753766, DOI 10.1126/science.adm8386); (iii) cell-type-restricted transcriptional control in a gene-therapy payload; or (iv) spatially localized delivery, such as focused-ultrasound BBB opening applied to selected regions, which produced numerically greater regional Abeta reduction in insonated versus contralateral homologous regions (Rezai et al., N Engl J Med 2024;390:55-62, PMID 38169490, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2308719). Distribution of a freely diffusing peptide in brain ISF is governed by diffusion, bulk flow and target binding, not by the designer's intent.
findings.required_fix: Deduplicate FULL_BRAIN_DRUGS_DATA: the four repeated sequences must either be collapsed into single entries or genuinely re-engineered so the sequences differ, and the conflicting Kd and pLDDT values must be removed since at most one value per pair can be correct. Add an automated uniqueness assertion at load time that throws if two records share a sequence. Then, for every record, replace the aspirational "targets" string with two explicit fields: "intended site of action" and "mechanism conferring selectivity for that site", where the second field must read "NONE -- distribution will be governed by ISF diffusion and target-mediated binding" unless a real mechanism (restricted receptor with cited expression data, vector tropism, or spatially localized delivery) is supplied. Finally, revise README.md:43-92 to state the actual number of distinct sequences.

findings.title: No proteolytic stability or plasma-half-life consideration; all 25 are unmodified linear L-peptides with free termini, predicted median human-serum t1/2 of 26 minutes
findings.evidence_location: app.js:143-391 (all 25 sequence fields -- every one is a plain string of standard L-amino acids with no modification notation); app.js:142,152,162,172,182 etc. (chemStruct fields describe only the natural-product warhead and linker chemistry -- "Cys-Lys Amide Coupling", "1,2,3-Triazole Linker", "Azide Linker" -- with no half-life-extension element); README.md:96-102 (ADMET section addresses hERG, seizure, cytokine storm and receptor desensitization, but not proteolysis, clearance or half-life); grep confirms zero occurrences of protease, peptidase, proteolysis, half-life, clearance (drug sense), or stability across all four files
findings.what_is_wrong: Every one of the 25 designs is an unmodified linear peptide of standard L-amino acids with a free N-terminus and free C-terminus. None is cyclized, none is N-methylated, none contains D-residues or beta-amino acids, none carries a PEG, an albumin-binding moiety, a lipid, or an Fc. The chemStruct fields describe only how the natural-product warhead is attached; there is no half-life-extension strategy anywhere. I applied the published Cavaco et al. human-serum half-life regression model (ln t1/2 = 2.226 + 0.053*NP% - 1.515*[Trp present] + 1.290*[>=2 Tyr] - 1.052*[pI >= 10]) to all 24 parseable sequences: predicted t1/2 ranges from 8 min (HippoDual-TrkB-AMPK-X5) to 100 min (AstroSuper-CBF-EAAT2-A5), median 26 min; 18 of 24 fall below 60 min and 24 of 24 below 120 min. Twenty-two of the 24 contain tryptophan, which the model identifies as the single largest destabilizing term, and four have pI >= 10, which is the second destabilizing term. The platform reports "Tolerance Downregulation < 4.2% after 30 days" (README.md:102) and "Tolerance Rate: 0.0%" (app.js:157) -- 30-day pharmacology assertions for molecules with a predicted plasma residence of tens of minutes and no stated dosing regimen.
findings.why_it_matters: Plasma half-life is the parameter that converts a required concentration into a required dose, and its absence is why the dosing arithmetic for these candidates is unbounded. For HippoAChE-AlkaPept-X2 with a predicted 27-min t1/2, Vd 0.1 L/kg and fu 0.05, sustaining 3xKd unbound brain concentration requires 16 g/day of synthetic peptide by continuous infusion at Kp,uu 0.01, versus 0.11 g/day under implausibly generous assumptions (t1/2 4 h, Vd 0.3, fu 0.5, Kp,uu 0.05). Approved synthetic peptide drugs are dosed in the range of roughly 0.001-10 mg/kg/day. A three-order-of-magnitude uncertainty that straddles the boundary between a manufacturable drug and a physical impossibility is not a detail; it is the go/no-go decision, and the platform provides no basis for making it. Separately, the "< 4.2% downregulation after 30 days" claim implies chronic sustained receptor occupancy that a minutes-scale half-life cannot produce under any plausible schedule.
findings.ground_truth: Cavaco et al. (Clin Transl Sci 2021;14:1349-1358, PMID 33641212, DOI 10.1111/cts.12985) curated 579 literature entries on peptide proteolytic lifetime and derived and validated a serum-t1/2 regression from unmodified peptides; their synthesized validation library spanned 7.4 to 403.4 minutes in human serum, with most peptides in the 30-60 min range. Unmodified linear peptides are cleaved by plasma aminopeptidases and carboxypeptidases from the free termini, by DPP-4 at position 2, and by neprilysin at hydrophobic residues, and are simultaneously cleared by glomerular filtration (a 3-5 kDa peptide is well below the ~60 kDa filtration threshold). Lau and Dunn (Bioorg Med Chem 2018;26:2700-2707, PMID 28720325, DOI 10.1016/j.bmc.2017.06.052) survey the >60 approved peptide drugs and the medicinal-chemistry strategies that made them viable: cyclization, N-methylation, D-amino-acid substitution, terminal capping, lipidation, PEGylation, and albumin or Fc fusion.
findings.required_fix: Add a predicted-serum-half-life field to every record, computed from the sequence with a cited model (the Cavaco regression is a reasonable, transparent starting point) and displayed with an explicit uncertainty range, not a point estimate. Add a paired "half-life extension strategy" field, populated with the specific modification proposed (N/C-terminal capping, head-to-tail or disulfide cyclization, D-residue or N-methyl substitution at identified cleavage sites, lipidation, PEG, albumin binder, or Fc fusion) or "NONE". Add an explicit dose-projection panel per candidate that propagates predicted t1/2, assumed Vd, assumed fu,plasma and a predicted Kp,uu range through to a required dose with its full uncertainty interval, so the reader sees the three-order-of-magnitude spread rather than a false precision. Finally, delete README.md:102 and app.js:157 ("Tolerance Downregulation < 4.2% after 30 days", "Tolerance Rate: 0.0%") -- these are 30-day claims with no dosing regimen behind them.

findings.title: Efficacy is ranked on binding free energy and Kd alone; Kp,uu,brain, fu,plasma, fu,brain and MDCK-MDR1 efflux ratio -- the actual determinants of CNS effect -- appear nowhere, and the reported dG and Kd values are mutually inconsistent by 3-4 orders of magnitude
findings.evidence_location: app.js:869-895 (renderLeaderboardTable ranks on pLDDT, dG and CEI); app.js:1049-1103 (renderBenchmarkChart plots "Cognitive Enhancement Index" against |dG|); app.js:124-135 (AF3_CANDIDATES: plddt, dg, cei only); app.js:146,156,166,176,186,198,208,218,228,238,250,260,270,280,290,302,312,322,332,342,354,364,374,384,394 (all 25 affinity strings, format "dG = X kcal/mol | Kd = Y nM | AF3 pLDDT = Z"); index.html:305,316 (leaderboard column headers); grep confirms zero occurrences of Kp, Kp,uu, unbound, fu, MDCK, MDR1, P-gp, efflux or Papp across all four files
findings.what_is_wrong: The platform's entire prioritization logic runs on affinity and structural confidence. The leaderboard (app.js:869-895) and the benchmark chart (app.js:1049-1103) rank candidates on pLDDT, dG and an undefined "Cognitive Enhancement Index"; not one exposure parameter enters the ranking. There is no unbound brain-to-plasma partition coefficient, no plasma or brain unbound fraction, no efflux-transporter assessment, and no in-vitro permeability estimate anywhere in the codebase. Secondarily, the two affinity numbers reported for each candidate are not consistent with one another: at 298 K, dG = -18.4 kcal/mol (app.js:146) corresponds to Kd = 3.2e-5 nM, not the stated 0.32 nM -- a factor of ~9,900. Across five spot-checked records the discrepancy ranges from 670x to 15,800x, always in the direction of the stated Kd being weaker than the stated dG implies, which indicates the two numbers were assigned independently rather than derived from one another.
findings.why_it_matters: Ranking CNS candidates on affinity is the classic way to advance the wrong molecule. Two candidates differing tenfold in Kd but hundredfold in Kp,uu,brain will have opposite efficacy orderings, and this platform would rank them backwards with full confidence. Because affinity is the only input, the leaderboard at app.js:869-895 is not merely incomplete -- it is actively anti-correlated with the property that matters for polar, high-molecular-weight polypeptides, where the exposure term dominates by orders of magnitude and the affinity term barely moves. The dG/Kd inconsistency compounds this: since Kd is the quantity that feeds any target-engagement or dose calculation, and it disagrees with the reported dG by up to four orders of magnitude, no dose can be derived from the platform's own numbers even in principle.
findings.ground_truth: The correct efficacy metric for CNS drugs is the unbound brain concentration relative to target potency, which requires Kp,uu,brain = Cu,brain / Cu,plasma -- not total brain concentration, which is confounded by nonspecific lipid and tissue binding and is the single most common error in CNS DMPK. Loryan et al. (Pharm Res 2022;39:1321-1341, PMID 35411506, DOI 10.1007/s11095-022-03246-6) surveyed European and US pharma and report that 93% have established a common cross-disciplinary understanding of Kp,uu,brain and 79% describe its implementation as "game-changing" for their portfolios; the paper also documents the accepted toolbox. The minimum honest in-silico DMPK layer for a platform like this is: (1) predicted Kp,uu,brain reported as a distribution or credible interval, never a point estimate; (2) predicted fu,plasma, with an explicit note that polycations bind albumin, alpha-1-acid glycoprotein and glycosaminoglycans; (3) predicted fu,brain from a brain-homogenate binding model; (4) an MDCK-MDR1 bidirectional efflux ratio, with ER > 2-2.5 flagged as P-gp-substrate risk, plus a BCRP assessment; (5) predicted passive permeability (Papp); and (6) a propagated target-engagement calculation from dose to Cu,brain/Kd carrying all upstream uncertainty. For a 3-5 kDa hydrophilic polypeptide, several of these predictors are outside their applicability domain, and the honest output is a wide interval plus an explicit out-of-domain warning -- which is far more useful than a fabricated point value. Thermodynamically, dG = RT ln(Kd) at T = 298 K with RT = 0.5924 kcal/mol; the two quantities must be derived from one another.
findings.required_fix: Replace the affinity-only leaderboard ranking (app.js:869-895) with a composite that requires an exposure term, and refuse to rank any candidate for which Kp,uu,brain has not been estimated -- show it as unranked rather than assigning it a position. Add to every record: predicted Kp,uu,brain with a credible interval, predicted fu,plasma, predicted fu,brain, predicted MDCK-MDR1 efflux ratio, and predicted Papp, each with an explicit applicability-domain flag for out-of-range molecules. Every one of these should be rendered as an interval, and where the model does not apply to a 4 kDa polypeptide, render "OUT OF DOMAIN" rather than a number. Separately, fix the dG/Kd inconsistency: derive one from the other with the stated temperature (Kd = exp(dG/RT), RT = 0.5924 kcal/mol at 298 K) and display the temperature, or remove one of the two quantities. Finally, define "Cognitive Enhancement Index" or remove it -- it is currently an undefined score driving a chart at app.js:1063 and a leaderboard column at index.html:306.

findings.title: Developability and CMC are unassessed and the advertised "Copy FASTA -> Launch AlphaFold Server" workflow will emit invalid input: 11 of 25 sequences have odd cysteine counts, two contain the non-standard letter B, and one "sequence" is an English phrase
findings.evidence_location: app.js:381 (AstroPafr-Block-A4, sequence field = "His14-Phe174-Linker-Peptide-Conjugate"); app.js:173 and app.js:371 (CKCHGMSGSCSTKTCWWG**B**LCPFRRACPDCH -- B is the Asx ambiguity code, not an amino acid) and app.js:130 (same B in AF3 candidate CogWnt-Fzd-09 fasta); odd-Cys candidates at app.js:163 (2C, even), 173 (7C), 195 (6C, even) -- specifically ids 3,4,7,9,12,13,15,16,17,20,22,23 with odd or high counts, e.g. app.js:173 and 371 (7 Cys in a 31-mer), app.js:205 and 361 (7 Cys in a 37-mer), app.js:143 and 215 (8 Cys); app.js:660-671 (copyModalFasta) and index.html:362-363 (Copy FASTA / Launch AlphaFold Server buttons); app.js:648-652 (initModal3DCanvas, renderModalPlddtChart, renderModalPaeHeatmap all invoked on drug.sequence unconditionally)
findings.what_is_wrong: Three concrete defects, all of which are developability signals as well as software bugs. (1) app.js:381 sets sequence to the literal string "His14-Phe174-Linker-Peptide-Conjugate". This is not a sequence. The modal nevertheless renders a 3D backbone (app.js:674-773), a residue-level pLDDT curve (app.js:775-832) and a PAE heatmap (app.js:834-866) from it, because all three functions index into the string blindly; the pLDDT chart will produce axis labels like "H1 i2 s3 -4 15 44". The Copy FASTA button (app.js:660) will place this English phrase on the clipboard for submission to AlphaFold Server. (2) Two records (app.js:173, app.js:371) and one AF3 candidate (app.js:130) contain the letter B in "TCWWGBLCPFRRACPDCH". B is the IUPAC ambiguity code for Asx (Asp or Asn) and is not a synthesizable residue; AlphaFold Server rejects non-standard single-letter codes. (3) Eleven of the 25 sequences have an odd number of cysteines, including several with very high cysteine density -- 7 Cys in a 31-mer (app.js:173, 371), 7 Cys in a 37-mer (app.js:205, 361), 8 Cys in a 47-mer (app.js:143) and 8 in a 45-mer (app.js:215). An odd count guarantees at least one unpaired free thiol. Nowhere in the codebase is a disulfide connectivity specified, nor is oxidative folding, scrambling, dimerization, or thiol-mediated aggregation discussed.
findings.why_it_matters: The Copy-FASTA-and-launch-AlphaFold-Server workflow is one of the genuinely honest features of this platform, and these defects break it in exactly the cases a user is most likely to try. A user clicking Copy FASTA on AstroPafr-Block-A4 gets an English phrase; on AstroZo1-Protect-A3 or HippoWnt-FzdAgonist-X4 they get a string AlphaFold Server will reject. On the science side, the free-thiol problem is a real and underappreciated developability killer for cysteine-dense peptides: with 7 cysteines in a 31-mer there are 105 possible disulfide pairings for six of them plus a free thiol, so oxidative refolding yields a heterogeneous mixture rather than a single species. That mixture is not characterizable, not manufacturable to a specification, prone to intermolecular disulfide dimerization and aggregation on storage, and -- because aggregates are the dominant driver of anti-drug-antibody responses -- directly contradicts the unsupported "Immunogenicity: Low" labels at app.js:167, 271 and 303. None of this appears anywhere; the platform reports a single pLDDT and a single Kd as though a single, unambiguous molecule existed.
findings.ground_truth: AlphaFold Server accepts only the 20 standard single-letter amino-acid codes for protein chains; B, Z, J and X are rejected. For disulfide-containing peptides, the manufacturable design requires an even cysteine count with explicitly specified pairwise connectivity, a defined oxidative folding route, and demonstration of a single predominant regioisomer. Unpaired cysteines in a therapeutic peptide are conventionally either removed, substituted (to Ser or alpha-aminobutyric acid), or deliberately capped, precisely to prevent scrambling and thiol-mediated dimerization. Standard developability triage for peptides includes: sequence validation, disulfide connectivity assignment, predicted and measured solubility, predicted aggregation propensity, oxidation/deamidation liability scanning (Met, Trp, Asn-Gly, Asp-Pro), and an aggregation-linked immunogenicity risk assessment. The 25 sequences here are Trp-rich and several contain Asn-Gly, so oxidation and deamidation liabilities are present and unexamined.
findings.required_fix: Add a validation function that runs over FULL_BRAIN_DRUGS_DATA and AF3_CANDIDATES at load time and rejects or visibly flags any sequence containing a character outside the 20 standard codes. Fix app.js:381 by supplying a real sequence or, if none exists, by rendering the card with an explicit "no sequence defined" state and disabling the 3D/pLDDT/PAE renderers and the Copy FASTA button for that record. Remove the B at app.js:130, 173 and 371 and replace with the intended D or N. For every cysteine-containing sequence, add an explicit disulfide-connectivity field and flag every odd cysteine count with a "FREE THIOL -- disulfide scrambling and dimerization risk" warning; for the 7-Cys and 8-Cys candidates, either specify the connectivity or reduce the cysteine count. Add a developability panel per candidate covering predicted solubility, predicted aggregation propensity, and Met/Trp oxidation and Asn-Gly deamidation liabilities, and remove the unsupported "Immunogenicity: Low / Very Low" strings at app.js:167, 271 and 303 in favour of "NOT ASSESSED".

literature.title: Brain delivery of therapeutic proteins using an Fc fragment blood-brain barrier transport vehicle in mice and monkeys
literature.what_it_provides: The Denali antibody transport vehicle (ATV): an engineered Fc fragment evolved to bind the apical domain of human transferrin receptor without amino acid insertions, deletions or unnatural appendages. A crystal structure confirms the TV binding site is distinct from the transferrin and FcRn sites. Anti-BACE1 ATV given peripherally to hTfR-knockin mice and cynomolgus monkeys produced substantially improved CNS uptake and sustained pharmacodynamic responses. The platform accommodates bispecifics and protein fusions.
literature.how_to_apply_here: This is the concrete answer to what the 25 candidates are missing. Any of these peptide binders intended for a parenchymal CNS target must be reformatted as a fusion to a TfR1-binding transport vehicle rather than delivered as a naked peptide. It also supplies the correct experimental readouts the platform should be projecting -- brain uptake and target-engagement pharmacodynamics in an hTfR-knockin model -- instead of pLDDT and dG.

literature.title: Delivery of the Brainshuttle amyloid-beta antibody fusion trontinemab to non-human primate brain and projected efficacious dose regimens in humans
literature.what_it_provides: Roche's Brainshuttle module fused to gantenerumab. A single 10 mg/kg IV dose of trontinemab in NHP versus 20 mg/kg gantenerumab gave increased brain endothelial and parenchymal uptake with more homogeneous distribution; nonlinear mixed-effects PK modelling with correction for tissue residual blood estimated a 4-18-fold increase in brain exposure. A clinical PK/PD model of gantenerumab was extended with a brain compartment driving plaque removal, allometrically scaled from NHP, and used to predict first-in-human dosing.
literature.how_to_apply_here: This is the exact template for the PK/PD layer this platform lacks: shuttle-enabled brain exposure, quantified fold-change with residual-blood correction, linked to a mechanistic brain-compartment PK/PD model, and used to project a human dose regimen. Building even a simplified version of this per candidate would convert DMPK-01 and DMPK-07 from blockers into a real deliverable.

literature.title: Receptor-mediated drug delivery of bispecific therapeutic antibodies through the blood-brain barrier
literature.what_it_provides: Quantitative brain-uptake benchmarks I verified directly in the full text: unmodified antibody uptake of 0.07 %ID/g (murine precursor of bapineuzumab) and 0.028 %ID/g (mAb158) in mouse; IgG in primate brain <0.01% of the plasma concentration; control mouse IgG2a brain VD of 11 uL/g, i.e. confined to the brain plasma volume. Against these, RMT-enabled molecules: chimeric HIRMAb 2.0 +/- 0.1 %ID/100 g in Rhesus at 2 h; cTfRMAb-AbetaScFv bispecific 3 %ID/g in mouse; 8D3 and RI7-217 TfR antibodies 3.1 +/- 0.4 and 1.6 +/- 0.2 %ID/g at 60 min. Reviews the TfR, insulin receptor, IGF1R and leptin receptor RMT systems.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Supplies the hard numbers for the calibration argument in DMPK-02: the platform's 25 naked polypeptides will not exceed an unmodified IgG's 0.03-0.07 %ID/g, and the 20-100x gap to RMT-enabled molecules is the size of the problem the designs ignore. These are the reference values to display alongside any predicted brain exposure on the platform.

literature.title: Treatment of Alzheimer's Disease and Blood-Brain Barrier Drug Delivery
literature.what_it_provides: States that 98% of small-molecule drugs and ~100% of biologic drugs do not cross the BBB, and that in 2020 fewer than 1% of all Alzheimer's drug development projects incorporated a BBB delivery technology -- identifying the omission of delivery technology as a primary structural cause of AD drug-development failure.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Directly diagnoses this platform's failure mode. CognitionBioChem is a well-executed instance of the >99% of AD programs that Pardridge identifies as lacking any BBB delivery technology. Citing it in the README would let the project position itself honestly relative to the field's known central obstacle rather than silently reproducing it.

literature.title: Unbound Brain-to-Plasma Partition Coefficient, Kp,uu,brain -- A Game Changing Parameter for CNS Drug Discovery and Development
literature.what_it_provides: A 47-question survey of DMPK organizations across major European and US pharmaceutical companies (Bayer, Vertex, Lundbeck, Biogen, AbbVie, Novartis, Janssen, Sanofi, Boehringer, Roche, Pfizer, AstraZeneca, GSK, Novo Nordisk). 93% report an established cross-disciplinary understanding of Kp,uu,brain; 79% describe its implementation as 'game-changing' for their portfolio; 74% consider the current toolbox for Kp,uu assessment and validation satisfactory for discovery and early development. Documents accepted methodology and its limitations.
literature.how_to_apply_here: This is the authority for DMPK-07: Kp,uu,brain, not affinity and not total brain concentration, is the industry-standard CNS efficacy metric. It defines the minimum parameter set the platform must add (Kp,uu,brain, fu,plasma, fu,brain) and establishes that a CNS platform ranking on dG alone is out of step with essentially the entire industry.

literature.title: An AAV capsid reprogrammed to bind human transferrin receptor mediates brain-wide gene delivery
literature.what_it_provides: BI-hTFR1, an engineered AAV capsid binding human TfR1, actively transported across human brain endothelial cells; 40-50x greater CNS reporter expression than AAV9 in human-TfR1 knockin mice, with the enhanced tropism CNS-specific and absent in wild-type mice. Delivery of GBA1 substantially increased brain and CSF glucocerebrosidase activity over AAV9.
literature.how_to_apply_here: The state of the art for genetically encodable CNS payloads, and directly relevant to DMPK-05. Several of these designs are pure peptides that could in principle be expressed rather than infused, and the CNS-specific-versus-wild-type contrast is the cleanest published demonstration of what genuine mechanism-backed CNS targeting looks like -- the standard against which the platform's unmechanized region assignments should be judged.

literature.title: Ultrasound Blood-Brain Barrier Opening and Aducanumab in Alzheimer's Disease
literature.what_it_provides: Clinical demonstration in three participants of focused ultrasound applied with each of six monthly aducanumab infusions to transiently open the BBB in selected brain regions; Abeta reduction measured by F-18 florbetaben PET was numerically greater in insonated regions than in the contralateral homologous untreated regions, with safety and cognitive follow-up over 30-180 days.
literature.how_to_apply_here: The only clinically demonstrated route to genuine region-selective enhancement of CNS drug delivery, and therefore the honest counterpoint to this platform's unmechanized 'five brain regions' claim (DMPK-05). If regional selectivity is central to the project's thesis, FUS is a real mechanism that could deliver it -- but it must be stated as the mechanism, with its own dosing and safety implications.

literature.title: Discovery of Novel Blood-Brain Barrier Targets to Enhance Brain Uptake of Therapeutic Antibodies
literature.what_it_provides: Transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of mouse brain endothelial cells identified basigin, Glut1 and CD98hc as highly abundant candidate RMT targets. Antibodies against each were significantly enriched in brain after in-vivo dosing; anti-CD98hc showed robust brain accumulation and a significant pharmacodynamic response measured as brain Abeta reduction. Also establishes the negative result that literature-nominated targets and microarray-identified BBB-enriched proteins failed to give meaningful uptake because of low protein abundance.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Provides the second validated RMT pathway (CD98hc) as an alternative to TfR1, useful because TfR1 shuttles carry reticulocyte and iron-homeostasis liabilities. The negative-result half is equally instructive for this platform: target selection based on literature assertion rather than measured endothelial protein abundance produced no brain uptake -- exactly the failure mode of asserting cell-type targets without expression data.

literature.title: Estimating peptide half-life in serum from tunable, sequence-related physicochemical properties
literature.what_it_provides: A meta-analysis of 579 curated literature entries on peptide proteolytic lifetime, yielding a validated multivariable regression for human-serum terminal half-life of unmodified peptides: ln t1/2 = 2.226 + 0.053*(% nonpolar residues) - 1.515*(Trp present) + 1.290*(>=2 Tyr) - 1.052*(pI >= 10). Validated against a synthesized 16-peptide library spanning 7.4-403.4 min in human serum and against 21 clinical-stage peptides.
literature.how_to_apply_here: I applied this model directly to all 24 parseable sequences to produce the predicted median 26-minute serum half-life in DMPK-06. It is transparent, sequence-only, requires no new data, and could be implemented in the platform in a few lines of JavaScript -- making it the cheapest possible first step toward an honest PK layer. Its coefficients also tell the designers what to change: reduce Trp, avoid pI >= 10, both of which these sequences violate systematically.

literature.title: Therapeutic peptides: Historical perspectives, current development trends, and future directions
literature.what_it_provides: Comprehensive review of the peptide therapeutic landscape from a curated dataset of peptides that have entered human clinical studies (>150 in active development, >60 approved in the US and other major markets), covering molecular characteristics, regulatory benchmarks, and therapeutic-area distribution.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Establishes the realistic envelope for a synthetic peptide drug -- size, dose, route, and the stabilization chemistry that successful peptides carry -- against which these 25 unmodified 26-47-mers can be honestly benchmarked. Useful for DMPK-06 in choosing a specific half-life-extension strategy, and for setting a defensible upper bound on manufacturable daily dose.

literature.title: Lipid selectivity in novel antimicrobial peptides: Implication on antimicrobial and hemolytic activity
literature.id: PMID 28236791; DOI 10.1016/j.colsurfb.2017.02.003; Colloids Surf B Biointerfaces 153:152-159
literature.what_it_provides: Two closely related designed peptides differing in hydrophobic moment and net charge: P6 showed no antimicrobial activity but high hemolytic activity, P6.2 showed good antibacterial and low hemolytic activity. Surface-pressure and zeta-potential measurements attribute the difference to relative affinity for zwitterionic PC (mammalian, erythrocyte-like) versus anionic PG membranes, and show P6's higher erythrocyte-membrane affinity drives its hemolysis.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Modern demonstration that hemolytic liability in cationic amphipathic peptides is tunable by, and predictable from, hydrophobic moment and charge -- the two parameters I computed in DMPK-03. Supplies both the mechanistic rationale for flagging muH 0.88-0.89 at charge +5 to +9 as a hemolysis risk, and the experimental design (erythrocyte-membrane affinity plus HC50) that the platform must run before claiming '0% risk'.

literature.title: Peptide hydrophobicity controls the activity and selectivity of magainin 2 amide in interaction with membranes
literature.what_it_provides: Magainin-2 amide analogues designed with varying hydrophobicity but deliberately conserved hydrophobic moment, net charge and hydrophilic-helix angle. Permeabilization of anionic PG vesicles was insensitive to hydrophobicity, whereas permeabilization of PC-rich (mammalian-like) vesicles increased sharply with it; antibacterial and hemolytic activity both increased with hydrophobicity, and a strong correlation was found between hemolytic effect and PC-vesicle permeabilization.
literature.how_to_apply_here: The foundational controlled-variable experiment behind the hydrophobicity-hemolysis relationship used in DMPK-03. Older than the 10-year window but cited deliberately because it is the cleanest isolation of the causal variable, and because it directly refutes the platform's stated rationale at README.md:99 that hydrophobic peptide character protects against membrane-mediated toxicity -- in this class, hydrophobicity is the driver of mammalian membrane lysis, not a shield.

reviews.discipline: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
reviews.reviewer_persona: PhD in cheminformatics/ML, 14 years building and validating ADMET and toxicity prediction models in pharma (hERG, seizure liability, hepatotox, peptide developability); published on model calibration, conformal prediction and applicability-domain estimation for regulatory-facing QSAR.

findings.title: The entire "In Silico ADMET & Safety" layer is 25 hardcoded prose strings — there is no model, no descriptor calculation, no data source, and no computation of any kind
findings.evidence_location: app.js:147, 157, 167, 177, 187, 199, 209, 219, 229, 239, 251, 261, 271, 281, 291, 303, 313, 323, 333, 343, 355, 365, 375, 385, 395 (all 25 `safety:` string literals); sole consumer at app.js:640 (`${drug.safety}` interpolated into innerHTML at app.js:606-643); README.md:96-102; index.html label at app.js:639 ("6. ADMET Safety Profile & Side Effects")
findings.what_is_wrong: Every safety number in the platform is a string literal typed into a JavaScript array. I traced the data flow end to end: `drug.safety` is written at 25 places and read at exactly one (app.js:640), where it is pasted verbatim into the modal HTML. Nothing parses it, derives it, or checks it. A repo-wide grep for any ADMET machinery returned zero hits outside the section heading itself: no `rdkit`, `chemprop`, `deepchem`, `sklearn`, `xgboost`, no `fetch`/`XMLHttpRequest`/API call, no descriptor code, no `Math.random`, no model file, no training data, no reference dataset. The repo's only non-UI files are README.md, app.js, index.html, styles.css and a memory spec. The distribution of the literals betrays their origin: 25/25 rows carry the identical hERG value (24x "hERG IC50 > 50 μM", 1x the same value with "(0% Cardiotoxicity)" appended); Seizure Index appears in 21/25 rows and takes only 3 distinct values {0.00 (9x), 0.01 (8x), 0.02 (4x)}; and the third endpoint slot uses 22 different, mutually incomparable labels across 25 rows. No predictive model produces a point-identical value for 25 chemically distinct entities.
findings.why_it_matters: README.md:98 states "All 25 candidates underwent rigorous computational safety screening" and README.md:96 titles the section "In Silico ADMET & Safety Risk Profile Assessment". Both are false as written: no screening of any kind was performed. A reader — a collaborator, a reviewer, an investor, a student — is being told that a computational safety assessment exists and returned clean results. It does not exist. Every downstream finding in this review is a consequence of this one: the platform's central ADMET claim has no referent. In a therapeutics context this is the failure mode that gets programs killed and reputations destroyed, because the numbers are specific enough (0.01, 4.2%, 50 μM, 99.5/100) to be quoted by someone who assumes they came from somewhere.
findings.ground_truth: An in-silico ADMET assessment is a reproducible artifact: input structures (SMILES/sequence), a named model with a training set and a published validation, per-prediction output with uncertainty, an applicability-domain verdict, a version, and a timestamp. ADMET-AI (Swanson et al., Bioinformatics 2024, PMID 38913862) is the current open reference implementation for small molecules — Chemprop D-MPNN models trained on the 22 TDC ADMET datasets, runnable locally, emitting per-endpoint predictions plus a percentile against a DrugBank reference set. Nothing resembling this exists in the repo.
findings.required_fix: Delete every hardcoded `safety:` string and README.md:96-102 immediately, or replace the section body with an explicit banner: "Illustrative placeholder values. No ADMET model has been run. Not for decision-making." To make the claim real: (1) commit a script (`admet/run.py`) that reads structures from a manifest and calls a named model; (2) for the small-molecule warheads, run ADMET-AI or Chemprop v2 and emit JSON per compound with prediction, uncertainty and AD flag; (3) for the peptide conjugates, run the peptide-appropriate panel (see AIML-06/07) — hERG is not it; (4) write model name, version, training set, date and git SHA into every output record; (5) have app.js read that JSON rather than literals, and render "not assessed" where the pipeline produced nothing.

findings.title: "hERG IC50 > 50 μM (0% Risk)" — a 0% risk statement is never defensible, and the repo contains no exposure data, so the hERG safety margin that actually determines risk cannot be computed at all
findings.evidence_location: README.md:99; app.js:147 ("hERG IC50 > 50 μM (0% Cardiotoxicity)") and the identical value on app.js:157-395 (24 further rows); absence confirmed by grep over README.md, app.js, index.html for cmax|auc|clearance|half.?life|bioavailab|dose|mg/kg|plasma|pharmacokinet|intraven|subcutaneous — zero hits
findings.what_is_wrong: Three distinct errors. (a) "0% Risk" is a claim of certainty. No assay and no model yields zero risk; a hERG assay yields a concentration-response with a confidence interval, and a hERG model yields a probability. (b) hERG risk is not an IC50, it is a ratio. The convention is margin = hERG IC50 / free plasma Cmax. The repo reports the numerator and contains no denominator anywhere — I grepped every platform file for dose, route, Cmax, AUC, clearance, half-life and plasma concentration and found zero hits. With IC50 = 50 μM, a 30x legacy margin permits free Cmax up to 1.67 μM (8.24 mg/L for a 4943 Da peptide); the ROC-optimal 37x TdP threshold permits 1.35 μM (6.68 mg/L); the 50x QTc threshold permits 1.00 μM (4.94 mg/L). Whether these candidates clear those bars is unknown and unknowable from this repo. (c) The value is reported to a single significant figure with a ">" and no CI, and is byte-identical across 25 different molecules ranging from an 8-residue peptide to a 100-residue construct with different natural-product warheads — physically impossible as a measurement or a prediction.
findings.why_it_matters: An expert reading "0% Risk" concludes cardiac safety has been cleared. Cardiac safety is the single most common cause of late-stage attrition and post-marketing withdrawal; ICH S7B/E14 require an integrated risk assessment, not an IC50. Publishing a zero-risk cardiotoxicity claim with no exposure term and no uncertainty is the exact pattern that produces false reassurance. It also poisons the rest of the safety panel by implying the same rigor was applied there.
findings.ground_truth: Leishman, Abernathy & Wang (J Pharmacol Toxicol Methods 2020;105:106900, PMID 32768644) examined margins for 367 compounds against CredibleMeds TdP classes: mean margins were 4.8 (Known risk), 28 (Conditional), 71 (Possible) and 339 (Not listed); ROC-optimal thresholds were 37-fold for separating known-TdP from not-listed and 50-fold for QTc-positive vs QTc-negative — confirming the 2002 30-fold heuristic. Lehmann, Eggleston & Wang (Pharmacotherapy 2018;38:341-348, PMID 29380488) independently validated the hERG IC50:Cmax ratio against observed TdP incidence (correlation 0.312, 95% CI 0.205-0.476, p<0.0001). Modern ML hERG models output a calibrated probability of block with an interval and an applicability-domain verdict, not a binary clearance; conformal prediction is the standard way to attach guaranteed-coverage intervals (Alvarsson et al., J Pharm Sci 2021;110:42-49, PMID 33075380). Separately, note that every public hERG training set (e.g. the TDC hERG tasks used by ADMET-AI) contains small molecules of MW ~150-600; a 4943 Da polycationic peptide is categorically outside the applicability domain of all of them, so a model would have to abstain rather than return "safe".
findings.required_fix: Remove "0% Risk" and "0% Cardiotoxicity" from README.md:99 and app.js:147 — no restatement of them is acceptable. Replace the hERG field with either (a) "Not assessed — out of applicability domain for small-molecule hERG models" for the peptide conjugates, or (b) if the small-molecule warhead alone is being assessed, a calibrated output of the form "P(hERG blocker) = 0.18, 90% conformal interval [0.06, 0.41], AD: in-domain (Tanimoto-to-training 0.42)" with the model, version and training set named. Add an explicit statement that no margin can be reported because no exposure (dose, route, free Cmax) has been estimated, and that a margin is required before any cardiac-safety claim.

findings.title: The stated hERG mechanism is factually contradicted by the repo's own sequences, targets the wrong binding site for this modality, and ignores the one hERG route a polycationic peptide could actually take
findings.evidence_location: README.md:99 ("Hydrophobic peptide linkers sterically prevent binding to hERG pore Tyr652/Phe656"); contradicted by the actual linkers at app.js:183 (MCVCDRENP**GGGGS**FLRRFWRR...), app.js:235 (...FRDVW**GGGGS**GCPWEC...), app.js:277 (...GAIIGLM**GGGSGGS**GRLVGHPW), app.js:287 (KWWKFLRR**GGGGS**MCVCDRENP**GGGGS**CDERACPRCHGF), app.js:339, app.js:391, and app.js:125-126,129 (AF3 candidate FASTA using GGGGSGGGGSGGGGS / GGSGGSGGSGGSGGS)
findings.what_is_wrong: The sentence is wrong three times over. (a) Its premise is false against its own data: every linker in the repo is a Gly-Ser linker (GGGGS or GGSGGS), the canonical *flexible hydrophilic* linker in fusion-protein engineering. Glycine and serine have Kyte-Doolittle values of -0.4 and -0.8; a GGGGS pentamer is among the least hydrophobic peptide segments constructible. There are no hydrophobic linkers in this platform. (b) The site named is the wrong one for the modality. Tyr652 and Phe656 sit on the S6 helices lining hERG's *inner* cavity, reached from the cytoplasmic face by small, lipophilic, typically basic amines that partition across the membrane. I computed GRAVY = -1.09 and net charge +8.98 at pH 7.4 for the 36-mer at app.js:153/247 — a strongly hydrophilic polycation of 4943 Da will not cross the plasma membrane and will never see Tyr652/Phe656. Arguing that a linker "sterically prevents" access to a site the molecule cannot reach in the first place is not a safety argument. (c) The route that *is* open to a polycationic peptide is the extracellular outer vestibule, and that is precisely the route the sentence does not address.
findings.why_it_matters: This is worse than an unsupported number: it is a mechanistic rationale that sounds authoritative and is verifiably false against the repo's own sequence data. A reader who checks the residues will conclude the author does not know how hERG block works; a reader who does not check will carry away a false mental model of why these molecules are safe. It also makes the "0% Risk" claim look like it was reasoned to rather than measured.
findings.ground_truth: Tyr652/Phe656 are the classic inner-cavity aromatic determinants of high-affinity small-molecule hERG block (Ala-scanning of S6 and the pore helix; see e.g. Mitcheson-type SAR literature). Peptides block hERG by an entirely different route: ErgTx binds the *outer* vestibule formed by the S5-P and P-S6 linkers, with cysteine-scanning identifying Trp585, Gly590, Ile593 and Pro632 as the critical positions (Pardo-Lopez et al., J Biol Chem 2002;277:16403-16411, PMID 11864985). BeKm-1, a 36-residue scorpion toxin, blocks hERG at low-nM potency through the outer mouth, and its activity depends on an indispensable arginine (Arg20) forming a salt bridge and hydrogen bonds with the channel vestibule — replacing it even with lysine dramatically reduces block (Zavarzina et al., FEBS Lett 2024;598:889-901, PMID 38563123). In other words: a ~4-5 kDa arginine-rich peptide is exactly the chemotype known to block hERG from the outside. The relevant assay is therefore an extracellular-application patch-clamp on hERG (and, given the polycation, a broader Kv/Nav/Cav panel), not a Tyr652/Phe656 docking argument.
findings.required_fix: Delete the mechanistic sentence at README.md:99 entirely. If a hERG statement is retained for the peptides, it must (a) name the outer-vestibule route as the plausible one, citing ErgTx/BeKm-1 precedent, (b) state that no extracellular hERG electrophysiology has been performed, and (c) list it as an open liability rather than a cleared one. Separately, correct any description of GGGGS as hydrophobic — it is the standard flexible hydrophilic linker.

findings.title: "Seizure Index = 0.01-0.02 / 1.0" is a fabricated metric — no such standardized index exists, and the best validated seizure-liability screens available reach only ~65% accuracy
findings.evidence_location: README.md:100; app.js:147, 157, 167, 177, 187, 199, 209, 219, 229, 239, 251, 261, 271, 281, 291, 313, 333, 355, 365, 385, 395 (21 of 25 rows carry a "Seizure Index" value); app.js:219 adds "(Capped Emax 135%)"; target classes at app.js:215-220 (NMDAR GluN2A), app.js:195-200 (α7 nAChR), app.js:257-262 (M1 mAChR), app.js:246-252 (AChE gorge block), app.js:32 (GABA_A)
findings.what_is_wrong: There is no standardized, published, validated 0-to-1 "Seizure Index" in preclinical safety pharmacology. I searched for one and found nothing of the kind; what exists are MEA-based in vitro seizure liability assays reporting multi-parameter electrophysiological fingerprints, and ion-channel panels reporting per-target IC30/EC30 values — neither collapses to a single normalized scalar. The values here are reported to two decimal places (0.00 / 0.01 / 0.02) with no units, no scale definition, no reference compounds, no assay, and only three distinct values across 21 molecules. Compounding the error, the reported near-zero values are asserted for molecules whose declared pharmacology is squarely proconvulsant: NMDAR GluN2A modulation (app.js:215-220), α7 nAChR potentiation (app.js:195-200), M1 muscarinic PAM activity with explicit M-current suppression and increased burst firing (app.js:257-262), and AChE inhibition claimed to raise synaptic ACh by +350% (app.js:252). Cholinergic overdrive and M-current block are textbook seizurogenic mechanisms. The mitigating claim at app.js:219 and README.md:100 — "Capped Emax 135%" — is itself an unsupported number: an Emax requires a fitted concentration-response curve, and no dose-response data exists in the repo.
findings.why_it_matters: CNS drugs are killed by seizure liability, and seizure is among the most severe FDA black-box neurotoxicity warnings. Presenting a precise-looking scalar near zero for a portfolio built entirely on cholinergic and glutamatergic amplification inverts the actual risk signal: the pharmacology described is the pharmacology that causes convulsions. An expert reading this sees a fabricated reassurance placed exactly where the highest concern should be flagged.
findings.ground_truth: State of the art is (i) in vitro MEA-based seizure liability assays on rodent cortical or hiPSC-derived neuronal networks, scored on multi-parameter spike-train fingerprints against known seizurogenic and negative controls (Bradley et al., Toxicol Sci 2018;163:240-253, PMID 29432603), and (ii) automated-electrophysiology ion-channel panels. The performance ceiling is modest and must be stated: Cohen et al. (Toxicol Sci 2025;203:253-268, PMID 39661496) evaluated an 11-target panel (Cav2.1, Cav3.2, GlyRA1, AMPA, HCN1, Kv1.1, Kv7.2/7.3, NaV1.1, NaV1.2, GABA-A, NMDA) against 34 preclinical compounds and 45 approved drugs; the integrated panel predicted convulsion in nonclinical species with sensitivity 68%, specificity 56% and accuracy 65%, with Cav2.1 the single most informative target. A field whose best integrated assay reaches 65% accuracy cannot support a per-compound scalar reported to 0.01 resolution.
findings.required_fix: Delete "Seizure Index" from README.md:100 and all 21 app.js rows — it is not a real metric and cannot be repaired by rescaling. Replace with an honest qualitative risk statement that reflects the declared pharmacology: flag every AChE-inhibitor, α7 nAChR PAM, M1 PAM and NMDAR-modulating candidate as *elevated* seizure concern pending assay. If a quantitative claim is wanted, run the Cohen-style ion-channel panel or an hiPSC-neuron MEA assay and report per-target IC30/EC30 with the panel's published sensitivity/specificity attached to any resulting call. Delete "Capped Emax 135%" unless a fitted concentration-response curve with the fit parameters is committed alongside it.

findings.title: "Tolerance Downregulation < 4.2% after 30 days" cannot be produced by any in-silico method, and the biased-agonism/recycling-endosome rationale offered for it has none of the measurements it requires
findings.evidence_location: README.md:102 ("Receptor Desensitization: Tolerance Downregulation < 4.2% after 30 days. Biased agonist signaling redirects receptors to recycling endosomes."); app.js:147 ("Downregulation: < 3.5%"), app.js:157 ("Tolerance Rate: 0.0%"), app.js:187 ("Tolerance Downregulation: < 3.8%"), app.js:199 ("Receptor Desensitization: Low"), app.js:261 ("Desensitization: Safe")
findings.what_is_wrong: A 30-day receptor-downregulation percentage is a chronic in vivo pharmacodynamic endpoint. It requires repeated dosing in an animal over 30 days followed by receptor quantification at multiple timepoints — radioligand binding Bmax, cell-surface biotinylation, or quantitative immunoblot/immunohistochemistry in the target region — plus a matched vehicle arm. No simulation, docking score, or structure prediction produces this number; the repo contains no dosing regimen, no route, no species, no PK model, and no receptor-density data. Reporting it to one decimal place (4.2%, 3.5%, 3.8%) implies a measured mean. The proffered mechanism is equally unsupported: "biased agonist signaling redirects receptors to recycling endosomes" is a claim that requires, at minimum, (i) a quantified bias factor — ΔΔlog(τ/K_A) from the Black-Leff operational model fitted to at least two pathways against a reference agonist, (ii) β-arrestin recruitment assays (BRET/enzyme complementation) alongside the G-protein readout, and (iii) direct trafficking assays distinguishing Rab11-positive recycling from Rab7/lysosomal degradation. None of these appears anywhere. Separately, app.js:157 assigns "Tolerance Rate: 0.0%" to HippoAChE-AlkaPept-X2, whose declared mechanism (app.js:158) is enzyme inhibition of AChE plus blockade of Aβ fibrillogenesis — there is no receptor for it to downregulate, so the endpoint is not merely unmeasured, it is inapplicable.
findings.why_it_matters: Tolerance is the make-or-break question for any chronic cognitive-enhancement agent — it is why cholinesterase inhibitors and nicotinic agonists have disappointing durability. Presenting a sub-5% 30-day figure claims the field's central failure mode has been solved, on the basis of nothing. A reader deciding whether this approach is worth pursuing would be materially misled about the single most important risk to its thesis.
findings.ground_truth: Ligand bias must be quantified, not asserted: the accepted framework is the operational model applied per pathway with subsequent calculation of ΔΔlogR / ΔΔlog(τ/K_A) relative to a reference agonist, and the field has repeatedly shown that apparent bias is assay-, cell- and system-dependent. The link from biased signalling to tolerance runs through measured trafficking: work on delta-opioid receptor agonists established that agonist-specific *recycling*, not internalization per se, tracks with tolerance liability (e.g. differential association of receptor-Gβγ complexes with β-arrestin2 determining recycling bias, PMC6620903; ligand- and cell-dependent determinants of DOR internalization, PMC3952036). Chronic receptor downregulation itself is measured in vivo, not predicted. No published in-silico method outputs a percentage downregulation at a 30-day horizon.
findings.required_fix: Delete the numeric downregulation claims at README.md:102, app.js:147, app.js:157 and app.js:187, and delete the biased-agonism sentence. Replace with "Not assessed — requires chronic in vivo dosing and receptor quantification." If the biased-signalling hypothesis is to be retained as a *hypothesis*, state it as such and specify the experiments that would test it: dual-pathway concentration-response (G-protein and β-arrestin) with operational-model bias factors and 95% CIs, plus Rab11 vs Rab7 colocalization trafficking assays. Remove the tolerance field entirely from non-receptor targets such as the AChE inhibitors (app.js:157).

findings.title: "Low Immunogenicity" is asserted for 4-11 kDa foreign peptides with zero epitope analysis, and the justification offered conflates innate TLR4 signalling with adaptive anti-drug-antibody risk
findings.evidence_location: README.md:101 ("Cytokine Storm Potential: Low Immunogenicity. Microglia-targeting candidates actively suppress TLR4/MD2 immune activation."); app.js:167 ("Immunogenicity: Very Low"), app.js:271 ("Immunogenicity: Low"), app.js:303 ("Immunogenicity: Low"), app.js:323 ("Cytokine Storm Risk: 0%"), app.js:343 ("Cytokine Storm Risk: None"); absence confirmed by grep over README.md, app.js, index.html for MHC|epitope|NetMHC|EpiMatrix|ADA|anti-drug — zero hits
findings.what_is_wrong: Three problems. (a) No immunogenicity analysis was performed. The repo contains no MHC-II binding prediction, no T-cell epitope map, no ADA assessment. The scale of what is being waved through: the 36-mer at app.js:153/247 presents 22 overlapping 15-mer frames, all 22 of which contain a large hydrophobic residue (F/W/Y/L/I/V/M) in positions 1-6 and are therefore candidate P1-anchored MHC-II binders; the 100-mer at app.js:125 presents 86 frames, 53 of them with a candidate P1 anchor. Multiplied across HLA-DR, -DQ and -DP and their allotypes, "Low" is a verdict rendered over thousands of unscored peptide-allele pairs. (b) The two categories are conflated. "Cytokine Storm Potential" (innate, PRR-driven) and "Immunogenicity" (adaptive, MHC-II/CD4 T-cell-driven, producing anti-drug antibodies) are different mechanisms with different assays; suppressing TLR4/MD2 signalling does nothing to reduce MHC-II presentation of the drug's *own* sequence. The sentence at README.md:101 uses the second as evidence for the first. (c) The specific antigen chosen is the worst possible case for this claim. Candidate B4 (app.js:277) and AF3 candidate rank 5 (app.js:129) both present KLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLM — Aβ16-35 — as the therapeutic payload. Deliberately administering an Aβ epitope to elderly patients is not a low-immunogenicity proposition; it is the design that caused the AN1792 program to be abandoned.
findings.why_it_matters: ADA formation against peptide therapeutics reduces exposure, abolishes efficacy, and in a minority of cases causes hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis. Regulators expect an in-silico immunogenicity risk assessment as a routine step in the development path for biologics. Asserting "Low" without one — and doing so for a construct built around an Aβ autoantigen — would be flagged immediately by any biologics development group and undermines confidence in the whole safety panel.
findings.ground_truth: The standard workflow is: (1) exhaustive 15-mer sliding-window scoring against a broad HLA class II allele panel using NetMHCIIpan-4.3, which closes the accuracy gap across DR, DQ and DP loci using immunopeptidomics-trained ML (Nilsson et al., Sci Adv 2023;9:eadj6367, PMID 38000035); (2) epitope-cluster and regulatory-T-cell analysis, e.g. the EpiMatrix / ClustiMer / JanusMatrix pipeline, which additionally scores human homology and Treg-epitope content and is explicitly supported for peptide drugs (Mattei et al., mAbs 2024;16:2333729, PMID 38536724); (3) confirmatory ex vivo human PBMC / CD4 T-cell proliferation or HLA-DR-restricted assays; (4) a stated ADA risk category. On the Aβ payload specifically: in the Phase IIa AN1792 trial of active Aβ42 immunization, 6% of vaccinated patients developed meningoencephalitis and the program was abandoned (reviewed in Yang & Xiao, Curr Pharm Biotechnol 2015;16:484-491, PMID 25860060; also Panza et al., Curr Alzheimer Res 2011;8:808-817, PMID 21592055).
findings.required_fix: Remove all "Low/Very Low Immunogenicity" and "Cytokine Storm Risk: 0%/None" strings (README.md:101; app.js:167, 271, 303, 323, 343). Separate the two endpoints into distinct fields — innate/PRR activation and adaptive ADA risk — because they require different evidence. Run NetMHCIIpan-4.3 over every candidate sequence against a representative HLA-DR/DQ/DP panel, commit the raw per-frame scores, and report a hit-count-based risk tier with the allele coverage stated. Flag the Aβ16-35-containing candidates (app.js:277, app.js:129) as carrying a specific, precedented CNS autoimmune risk and cite AN1792.

findings.title: The liabilities that actually govern this modality — membrane lysis/hemolysis, mammalian cytotoxicity, aggregation, proteolytic instability, polypharmacology — are absent entirely, while an inapplicable liability (hERG) is reported for all 25
findings.evidence_location: Sequences at app.js:153 and app.js:247 (KWWKFLRRFWRRLKKYFEELWKKLAEKYFELLKKYG), app.js:329 (FLRRFWRRLKKYFEELWKKLAEKYFELLKKYG), app.js:183, README.md:61 (KWWKFLRR), README.md:64 (FLRRFWRR), README.md:74 (KWWKFLRRFWRR), app.js:131 (AF3 rank 7, same 36-mer); absence confirmed by grep over README.md, app.js, index.html for hemoly|haemoly|cytotox|aggregat|protease|proteoly — zero hits (the one "aggregates" hit at app.js:334 is an efficacy claim about Tau clearance)
findings.what_is_wrong: These sequences are cationic amphipathic peptides — the antimicrobial/cell-penetrating chemotype — and the platform reports none of the liabilities that define that class. My calculations (average residue masses; Eisenberg consensus hydrophobicity; α-helical 100°/residue moment; Henderson-Hasselbalch net charge at pH 7.4): KWWKFLRRFWRR (README.md:74) is 1865 Da, q = +5.99, μH = 0.989; FLRRFWRR (README.md:64) is 1237 Da, q = +3.99, μH = 1.068; the 36-mer at app.js:153/247 is 4943 Da, q = +8.98, 13 Lys+Arg vs 4 Asp+Glu, μH = 0.615. For calibration I ran the same code on reference lytic peptides: melittin μH = 0.353, LL-37 μH = 0.559, TAT(47-57) q = +7.99. The candidate peptides are as amphipathic as, or more amphipathic than, the canonical membrane-lytic references. Trp/Arg-rich cationic 8-12-mers of exactly this composition are a well-characterized engineered-AMP series. Yet the safety field for these molecules reports hERG (largely inapplicable, see AIML-03) and a fabricated Seizure Index, and is silent on: hemolysis (HC50 against human erythrocytes), mammalian cytotoxicity (HepG2/HEK293/primary neurons and astrocytes), off-target polypharmacology (polycations bind heparan sulfate proteoglycans, phosphatidylserine, nucleic acids and anionic membranes indiscriminately), peptide self-aggregation, and plasma/CSF proteolytic stability. I want to be precise rather than alarmist: this chemotype is not uniformly toxic — Deslouches et al. found WK12 and WR12 to have negligible hemolytic and cytotoxic effects up to 10x MIC — which is exactly the point. Whether a given cationic amphipathic peptide is lytic depends on charge, hydrophobicity, length and amphipathicity in ways that must be measured. It cannot be asserted, and it certainly cannot be inferred from a hERG number.
findings.why_it_matters: The safety panel is calibrated for the wrong modality. It reports the liability of small-molecule CNS drugs (hERG, seizure) for molecules that are peptides, and omits every liability specific to peptides. A reader comparing candidates on this panel is comparing them on axes that do not discriminate, while the axes that would discriminate — lysis, cytotoxicity, stability, aggregation — are invisible. For CNS delivery this is compounded: peptides of 4-5 kDa with strongly negative GRAVY do not cross the blood-brain barrier and are rapidly degraded in plasma, so even the efficacy premise is untested; but the immediate safety consequence is that a potentially hemolytic polycation is being presented with a clean bill of health.
findings.ground_truth: For a cationic amphipathic peptide the obligatory developability/safety panel is: (1) hemolysis — HC50 on fresh human RBCs, reported alongside the efficacious concentration as a therapeutic index; (2) mammalian cytotoxicity — MTT/LDH on at least one hepatic, one renal and one target-tissue primary line; (3) plasma and CSF proteolytic stability — t1/2 in human plasma and brain homogenate; (4) aggregation propensity — sequence-based predictors (TANGO/WALTZ/AGGRESCAN class) plus ThT and DLS; (5) off-target polypharmacology — at minimum a broad receptor/ion-channel safety panel plus heparin/PS binding, because polycations are promiscuous; (6) BBB permeability and route. Deslouches et al. (J Med Microbiol 2016;65:554-565, PMID 27046192) is the reference showing both that Trp/Arg 12-mers of this exact composition are potent membrane permeabilizers and that hemolysis must be assayed rather than assumed, since their WK12/WR12 series proved well tolerated up to 10x MIC while related sequences are not.
findings.required_fix: Add the peptide panel above as explicit fields in the data model, populated with "Not assessed" until measured — an honest gap is a scientific statement; an omitted liability is not. Simultaneously mark hERG as "Not applicable / out of domain" for the peptide conjugates rather than reporting a clean value. Compute and display, at no experimental cost, the sequence-derived descriptors that already flag the risk: length, MW, net charge at pH 7.4, GRAVY, and Eisenberg hydrophobic moment, with the melittin/LL-37 reference values shown for calibration. Add BBB penetration and plasma stability as open questions in README.md Section 3.

findings.title: Two candidates use Aβ16-35 / Aβ16-23 verbatim as the therapeutic payload and are labelled "Aβ Disruptor" with "Fibril Blockade: 100%" — the sequence used is one of the shortest known amyloid-*forming* fragments of Aβ, i.e. a seed, not a breaker
findings.evidence_location: app.js:277 (BasalAChE-Abeta-B4, sequence "KLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLMGGGSGGSGRLVGHPW"), app.js:275 (name "AChE-Aβ Fibril Disruptor"), app.js:281 ("Fibril Blockade: 100%"), app.js:282 (mechanism claim); app.js:129 (AF3 candidate rank 5, "CogAbeta-Clearer-08", fasta beginning "KLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLM..."); README.md:77 ("Aβ Disruptor (KLVFFAED)")
findings.what_is_wrong: I aligned the payload against Aβ42 (DAEFRHDSGYEVHHQKLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLMVGGVVIA): "KLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLM" is an exact match to residues 16-35, and "KLVFFAED" at README.md:77 is an exact match to residues 16-23. This is not an Aβ-derived inhibitor scaffold; it is a verbatim copy of the Aβ central hydrophobic cluster (KLVFFA, 16-21) *plus* the second hydrophobic region (GAIIGLM, 29-35) — the two segments that drive Aβ self-assembly. Aβ16-22 in isolation forms highly ordered antiparallel cross-β amyloid fibrils on its own. My physicochemical numbers are consistent: the B4 payload has GRAVY +0.26 and net charge +1.03, i.e. a near-neutral hydrophobic peptide, the regime that favors β-sheet self-assembly, in contrast to every other candidate in the portfolio. Administering this into a brain that already contains Aβ plaques is a seeding proposition. Labelling it a "Fibril Disruptor" with "Fibril Blockade: 100%" (app.js:281) inverts the direction of the effect, and "100%" is a fabricated completeness claim on top of it. Note also that the aggregation liability is invisible to the platform's safety panel, which for this molecule reports only hERG, Seizure Index 0.01, and the 100% fibril figure.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the single most dangerous design error in the portfolio, because it is directionally wrong rather than merely unsupported: the molecule proposed as a therapy is the fragment used experimentally to *nucleate* amyloid. A reader who takes the label at face value would pursue a construct whose most likely in vivo effect on the stated endpoint is the opposite of the intended one. It also carries the immunogenicity precedent from AIML-06 — dosing an Aβ epitope into elderly patients has a documented history of CNS adverse events.
findings.ground_truth: Balbach, Ishii, Antzutkin, Leapman, Rizzo, Dyda, Reed & Tycko (Biochemistry 2000;39:13748-13759, PMID 11076514) established by EM, X-ray powder diffraction, birefringence and solid-state 13C NMR that Ac-KLVFFAE-NH2 (Aβ16-22) forms genuine amyloid fibrils with a β-strand backbone extending from Leu17 through Ala21 and an antiparallel β-sheet organization, and describe it as "among the shortest fibril-forming fragments of full-length β-amyloid reported to date". Subsequent work confirmed the same for the uncapped peptide and mapped the assembly pathway (e.g. PMID 21309606, PMID 35134456). Peptides that actually *break* Aβ β-sheets are deliberately register-disrupted derivatives of the CHC — proline substitution, N-methylation, or D-amino acid backbones — not wild-type copies; the β-sheet-breaker literature is explicit that the disrupting modification, not the recognition sequence, provides the activity.
findings.required_fix: Withdraw both candidates (app.js:275-282 and app.js:129) or redesign the payload. If an Aβ-recognition element is genuinely wanted, replace the wild-type CHC with a register-disrupted analogue (proline or N-methyl substitution within LVFFA, or a D-enantiomer/retro-inverso backbone) and say explicitly which modification confers the breaker activity. Remove "Fibril Blockade: 100%" (app.js:281). Add aggregation propensity — sequence predictor plus ThT kinetics and seeded-aggregation assay against recombinant Aβ42 — as a mandatory safety endpoint for any candidate containing an amyloidogenic segment, and flag the Aβ16-35 payload as a seeding risk in README.md:77.

findings.title: No safety value in the platform carries uncertainty, an applicability-domain verdict, a model identity, or provenance — the four things that make a prediction usable
findings.evidence_location: app.js:147-395 (all 25 `safety:` literals); app.js:146-394 (the parallel `affinity:` literals, which report ΔG, Kd and pLDDT to 2-3 significant figures with the same absence); app.js:639-641 (rendering, which adds no qualifiers); README.md:96-102
findings.what_is_wrong: Every safety and affinity figure is a bare point estimate. There is no confidence interval, no standard error, no probability, no prediction set, no coverage level. There is no applicability-domain statement anywhere — critical here because the entities being scored (4-11 kDa polycationic peptides) fall outside the training distribution of every public small-molecule ADMET model. There is no model name, version, training set, or hyperparameter record. There is no timestamp, no git SHA, no input manifest. Structurally, the safety field also has no schema: I extracted the third endpoint slot across the 25 rows and found 22 distinct labels (Downregulation, Tolerance Rate, Tolerance Downregulation, Immunogenicity, Tumorigenicity, Receptor Desensitization, Desensitization, Off-target Binding, Excitotoxicity, Systemic Toxicity, Peripheral Side Effects, Fibril Blockade, Safety Plasticity Score, Safety Index, Sepsis Safety, Cytokine Storm Risk, Inflammatory Cytokine Suppression, Lysosomal Clearance, Vasodilation Rate, Glutamate Toxicity, Tau Hyperphosphorylation, Cerebral Edema, Edema Risk), so no two candidates report the same endpoint set and cross-candidate ranking on safety is impossible. Several of those labels are efficacy claims (Lysosomal Clearance +420%, Inflammatory Cytokine Suppression 98%, Vasodilation Rate +45%, Tau Hyperphosphorylation Suppressed) presented under a heading that says "ADMET Safety Profile & Side Effects".
findings.why_it_matters: Even if a real model were wired in tomorrow, a point estimate with no uncertainty and no domain check is not decision-grade — it is the failure mode that causes silent, confident errors on out-of-domain inputs, which is precisely the regime these molecules occupy. And the heterogeneous schema means the panel cannot serve its one legitimate purpose, which is comparing 25 candidates on a common safety axis.
findings.ground_truth: Conformal prediction is the standard, model-agnostic way to attach validity guarantees: it retrofits any QSAR model into a confidence predictor emitting prediction intervals (regression) or prediction sets (classification) at a user-specified confidence level, with error-rate guarantees and an applicability domain that is intrinsically linked to the underlying model (Alvarsson, Arvidsson McShane, Norinder & Spjuth, J Pharm Sci 2021;110:42-49, PMID 33075380; the framing of conformal prediction as an OECD-principles-compliant alternative to ad hoc AD definitions goes back to Norinder et al. 2014). Chemprop v1/v2 ship uncertainty quantification and calibration methods with the relevant metrics built in (Heid et al., J Chem Inf Model 2024;64:9-17, PMID 38147829). ADMET-AI (PMID 38913862) additionally contextualizes each prediction against a DrugBank reference percentile, which is the minimum interpretability affordance a portfolio panel should offer.
findings.required_fix: Define one fixed safety schema applied identically to all 25 candidates: {endpoint, value, uncertainty (interval + coverage level), model, model version, training set, applicability-domain verdict, date, git SHA} — with "not assessed" as a first-class allowed value. Wrap whatever model is adopted in inductive conformal prediction at a stated confidence level (90% is conventional) and render the interval, not just the point. Add an explicit AD check (e.g. maximum Tanimoto or embedding distance to the training set) and force abstention when out of domain rather than returning a value. Move all efficacy-flavored fields (Lysosomal Clearance, Cytokine Suppression, Vasodilation Rate, Tau Hyperphosphorylation, Fibril Blockade) out of the safety panel into an efficacy panel.

findings.title: Safety profiles are generated for inputs that are not sequences and for sequences containing non-standard residues, proving no validation layer touched the data
findings.evidence_location: app.js:381 (AstroPafr-Block-A4 `sequence: "His14-Phe174-Linker-Peptide-Conjugate"`) with a full safety profile at app.js:385; app.js:173 and app.js:371 (`CKCHGMSGSCSTKTCWWG**B**LCPFRRACPDCH`) and app.js:130 (AF3 rank 6 fasta, same `B`); consumers at app.js:648-652 → app.js:708-729 (3D topology), app.js:787-795 (pLDDT chart), app.js:844-865 (PAE heatmap)
findings.what_is_wrong: Candidate A4's `sequence` field contains the English string "His14-Phe174-Linker-Peptide-Conjugate", not a peptide sequence, yet it is assigned a complete ADMET profile at app.js:385 ("hERG IC50 > 50 μM | Seizure Index: 0.00 | Cerebral Edema: Prevented") and is passed unchecked into initModal3DCanvas, renderModalPlddtChart and renderModalPaeHeatmap, which will index it character-by-character and render a "pLDDT profile" for the letters in the word "Linker". Separately, three sequences contain the character `B`, which is the IUPAC ambiguity code for Asx (Asn/Asp) and is not a standard amino acid; AlphaFold Server would reject it, so these sequences demonstrably never went through the pipeline the platform claims. This is a small defect on its own but it is the cleanest available proof for AIML-01: a data set in which a prose string and an invalid residue code both pass through to a rendered safety profile has no validation layer, and therefore no pipeline.
findings.why_it_matters: It removes any remaining ambiguity about whether some upstream computation might have existed and merely been cached as strings. It also means the FASTA copy button (index.html:362) will hand a user an unsubmittable sequence for at least four candidates, wasting their time at the AlphaFold Server.
findings.ground_truth: Any sequence-consuming pipeline validates its input first: alphabet restricted to the 20 standard one-letter codes (with an explicit policy for B/Z/X/U/O), non-empty, length within model limits, and a hard failure — not a rendered chart — on violation. AlphaFold Server accepts only standard residues for protein chains.
findings.required_fix: Add a validator that runs over FULL_BRAIN_DRUGS_DATA and AF3_CANDIDATES at load: reject any `sequence`/`fasta` containing characters outside ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY, and reject non-sequence strings. Fix app.js:381 by supplying the real conjugate sequence or marking the entry as small-molecule-only and suppressing its sequence-derived panels. Resolve the `B` at app.js:130, 173 and 371 to N or D explicitly. Suppress the pLDDT/PAE/3D panels for any entry that fails validation rather than rendering a plot from invalid input.

literature.title: ADMET-AI: a machine learning ADMET platform for evaluation of large-scale chemical libraries
literature.what_it_provides: Open-source, locally runnable Chemprop-based ADMET prediction across the TDC endpoint suite (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity including hERG), with DrugBank-referenced percentile context; highest average rank on the TDC ADMET Leaderboard; one million molecules in 3.1 h locally.
literature.how_to_apply_here: This is the drop-in replacement for the 25 hardcoded strings, for the small-molecule natural-product warheads (Huperzine A, curcumin, baicalein, asiatic acid, ginkgolide B, ferulic acid). Run it from a committed script over the warhead SMILES, emit JSON per compound, and have app.js read that JSON. It will NOT cover the peptide conjugates — its training data is small molecules — which is itself the finding to report for those entries.

literature.title: Therapeutics Data Commons: Machine Learning Datasets and Tasks for Drug Discovery and Development
