literature.what_it_provides: The benchmark substrate for therapeutic ML: 66 AI-ready datasets across 22 learning tasks, including the ADMET benchmark group (hERG, CYP inhibition, Caco-2, BBB, clearance, LD50, DILI) with fixed scaffold splits and leaderboards.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Use the TDC ADMET benchmark group to establish what performance any adopted model actually achieves on each endpoint, and quote that performance next to every prediction shown in the UI. It also supplies the honest counterargument to the hERG claims: the hERG training sets are small molecules of MW ~150-600, so a 4.9 kDa peptide is out of domain and the model must abstain.

literature.title: Chemprop: A Machine Learning Package for Chemical Property Prediction
literature.what_it_provides: Reference D-MPNN implementation with built-in uncertainty quantification and calibration methods, transfer learning, and hyperparameter optimization; the model layer underneath ADMET-AI.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Use Chemprop's UQ/calibration facilities so every predicted safety endpoint ships with a calibrated uncertainty rather than a bare point value, directly remediating AIML-09. Pin the version and commit the trained checkpoint hash.

literature.title: Predicting With Confidence: Using Conformal Prediction in Drug Discovery
literature.what_it_provides: Practical introduction to conformal prediction as a model-agnostic layer producing prediction intervals (regression) and prediction sets (classification) with guaranteed error rates, and an applicability domain intrinsically linked to the underlying model — satisfying the OECD (Q)SAR principles.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Wrap whichever ADMET model is adopted in inductive conformal prediction at a stated confidence level (e.g. 90%), so the UI shows 'P(hERG blocker) = 0.18, 90% CP interval [0.06, 0.41], AD: out-of-domain' instead of '0% Risk'. This is the single change that would move the safety panel from indefensible to defensible.

literature.title: Revisiting the hERG safety margin after 20 years of routine hERG screening
literature.what_it_provides: Empirical re-derivation of the hERG safety margin across 367 compounds: mean IC50/free-Cmax margins of 4.8 (Known TdP risk), 28 (Conditional), 71 (Possible) and 339 (Not listed); ROC-optimal thresholds of 37-fold (TdP) and 50-fold (QTc), confirming the 2002 30-fold heuristic.
literature.how_to_apply_here: This is the ground truth against which 'hERG IC50 > 50 μM (0% Risk)' fails: risk is the ratio, not the numerator. Use it to state explicitly that with IC50 = 50 μM the free Cmax must stay below ~1.35 μM (37x) for the TdP margin to be met, and that the repo contains no exposure estimate at all.

literature.title: Validation and Clinical Utility of the hERG IC50:Cmax Ratio to Determine the Risk of Drug-Induced Torsades de Pointes: A Meta-Analysis
literature.what_it_provides: Independent meta-analytic validation that the hERG IC50:free-Cmax ratio correlates with observed TdP incidence (0.312, 95% CI 0.205-0.476, p<0.0001), with a negligible-risk ratio around 80.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Second, independent source establishing that the margin — not the IC50 — is the risk metric, and that risk is expressed as a graded incidence correlation, never as '0%'. Cite alongside Leishman when rewriting README.md:99.

literature.title: In vitro human ion channel assays predictive of drug-induced seizure
literature.what_it_provides: Evaluation of an 11-target ion-channel panel (Cav2.1, Cav3.2, GlyRA1, AMPA, HCN1, Kv1.1, Kv7.2/7.3, NaV1.1, NaV1.2, GABA-A, NMDA) by automated electrophysiology against 34 preclinical compounds and 45 approved drugs; the integrated panel predicts convulsion with sensitivity 68%, specificity 56%, accuracy 65%; Cav2.1 the most informative single target.
literature.how_to_apply_here: This is the performance ceiling that makes 'Seizure Index = 0.01/1.0' indefensible: the best integrated seizure screen in the field reaches 65% accuracy, so no method supports a per-compound scalar at 0.01 resolution. It also specifies the panel to actually run on the α7 nAChR, GluN2A, M1 and AChE-inhibitor candidates.

literature.title: In Vitro Screening for Seizure Liability Using Microelectrode Array Technology
literature.what_it_provides: MEA-based seizure liability screen on cryopreserved rat cortical neurons, scoring 12 spike-train parameters against 20 reference compounds spanning GABA-A antagonists, glycine receptor antagonists, ion channel blockers and muscarinic agonists; 16/17 seizurogenic or neurotoxic compounds detected.
literature.how_to_apply_here: The accepted new-approach methodology for seizure liability, and the concrete assay to substitute for the invented Seizure Index. Note that its readout is a multi-parameter fingerprint against reference compounds, not a normalized scalar — which is exactly why the platform's metric does not exist.

literature.title: Accurate prediction of HLA class II antigen presentation across all loci using tailored data acquisition and refined machine learning (NetMHCIIpan-4.3)
literature.what_it_provides: Current state-of-the-art pan-allele MHC class II binding/presentation predictor with closed performance gap across HLA-DR, -DQ and -DP, trained on large immunopeptidomics datasets and accommodating inverted binding modes.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Run over every candidate sequence as exhaustive 15-mer sliding windows against a representative DR/DQ/DP allele panel — 22 frames for the 36-mer at app.js:153, 86 for the 100-mer at app.js:125 — and replace 'Low Immunogenicity' with a hit-count-based risk tier and committed raw scores.

literature.title: In silico methods for immunogenicity risk assessment and human homology screening for therapeutic antibodies
literature.what_it_provides: Description of the ISPRI immunogenicity workflow — EpiMatrix epitope mapping, ClustiMer clustering, JanusMatrix human-homology/Treg-epitope analysis, OptiMatrix deimmunization — with normalized immunogenicity scoring, explicitly supported for peptide drugs as well as antibodies.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Supplies the second half of a credible ADA risk assessment beyond raw MHC-II binding: epitope clustering, human-homology screening, and a normalized comparative immunogenicity score. Directly applicable to the Aβ16-35-containing candidates at app.js:277 and app.js:129, where human homology is the specific concern.

literature.title: Amyloid fibril formation by A beta 16-22, a seven-residue fragment of the Alzheimer's beta-amyloid peptide, and structural characterization by solid state NMR
literature.what_it_provides: Definitive demonstration by EM, X-ray powder diffraction, birefringence and solid-state 13C NMR that Ac-KLVFFAE-NH2 forms ordered antiparallel cross-β amyloid fibrils on its own, with β-strand conformation from Leu17 through Ala21; described as among the shortest fibril-forming fragments of full-length Aβ.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Establishes that the payload of BasalAChE-Abeta-B4 (app.js:277, Aβ16-35) and AF3 candidate rank 5 (app.js:129) is an amyloid seed, not an amyloid disruptor, falsifying the 'Fibril Blockade: 100%' claim at app.js:281 and the 'Aβ Disruptor' label at README.md:77.

literature.title: Comparative functional properties of engineered cationic antimicrobial peptides consisting exclusively of tryptophan and either lysine or arginine
literature.what_it_provides: Systematic characterization of engineered Trp/Arg and Trp/Lys cationic peptides of 8-18 residues: membrane permeabilization by SPR and flow cytometry, plus hemolytic and tetrazolium cytotoxicity assays; WK12/WR12 showed negligible hemolysis up to 10x MIC while shorter/other analogues differ.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Defines the assay set missing from the platform for KWWKFLRRFWRR, FLRRFWRR and the 36-mer amphipathic helix (hemolysis HC50, mammalian cytotoxicity, membrane permeabilization), and supplies the calibrated caveat that this chemotype's lytic behaviour must be measured rather than assumed in either direction.

literature.title: Mapping the binding site of a human ether-a-go-go-related gene-specific peptide toxin (ErgTx) to the channel's outer vestibule
literature.what_it_provides: Cysteine-scanning mutagenesis of the hERG S5-P and P-S6 linkers identifying Trp585, Gly590, Ile593 and Pro632 as the determinants of peptide-toxin binding at the channel's outer vestibule — a site and mechanism entirely distinct from small-molecule inner-cavity block at Tyr652/Phe656.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Falsifies the mechanistic claim at README.md:99. If these polycationic peptides have any hERG liability it would be via the extracellular outer vestibule, which the platform's steric argument does not address; the corresponding assay is extracellular-application patch-clamp, not a Tyr652/Phe656 docking rationale.

literature.title: The scorpion toxin BeKm-1 blocks hERG cardiac potassium channels using an indispensable arginine residue
literature.what_it_provides: MD and ensemble docking model of the hERG-BeKm-1 complex showing Arg20 of the 36-residue toxin forming a simultaneous salt bridge and hydrogen bonds with the channel vestibule; the R20K mutant shows dramatically reduced hERG activity.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Direct counterexample to the implicit premise that a polycationic peptide cannot pose hERG risk: an arginine-rich ~4 kDa peptide is precisely the chemotype that blocks hERG at low nM, and it does so through an arginine. Cite when rewriting README.md:99 for the app.js:153/247 36-mer (q = +8.98, 13 K+R).

literature.title: New developments of clinical trial in immunotherapy for Alzheimer's disease
literature.what_it_provides: Review documenting that in the Phase IIa AN1792 trial of active Aβ42 immunization, 6% of vaccinated patients developed meningoencephalitis as an adverse effect, leading to abandonment of the program (corroborated by Panza et al., Curr Alzheimer Res 2011;8:808-817, PMID 21592055).
literature.how_to_apply_here: Clinical precedent falsifying 'Low Immunogenicity' for the Aβ-epitope-bearing candidates at app.js:277 and app.js:129. Any construct presenting Aβ16-35 to an elderly CNS population must carry an explicit CNS autoimmunity risk flag citing this history.

literature.title: Polaris: an industry-led benchmarking platform for machine learning in drug discovery (polarishub.io; associated call-to-action, Nature Machine Intelligence 6:1120-1121)
literature.what_it_provides: Community benchmarking hub and Python library providing domain-appropriate datasets, splits and evaluation protocols for drug-discovery ML, created specifically to address unrealistic benchmark performance and leakage in existing leaderboards.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Use alongside TDC to select and report evaluation protocols that are not leakage-prone, so that any performance figure quoted next to a safety prediction in this platform is defensible. Listed as unverified because I confirmed the hub and repository exist via web search but did not directly retrieve the associated paper record in this session.

reviews.overall_assessment:
**Verdict: the ADMET/safety layer does not exist. It is 25 hardcoded prose strings, and the README sentence claiming "All 25 candidates underwent rigorous computational safety screening" (README.md:98) is false as written.**

I traced the complete data flow. `drug.safety` is written at 25 literal positions (app.js:147-395) and read at exactly one (app.js:640), where it is interpolated into the modal HTML. Nothing computes it. A repo-wide grep for RDKit, chemprop, DeepChem, scikit-learn, XGBoost, any HTTP call, or any descriptor code returns zero hits outside the section heading itself. The literals betray themselves statistically: 25/25 rows carry a byte-identical hERG value; "Seizure Index" appears in 21/25 rows with only three distinct values {0.00, 0.01, 0.02}; and the third endpoint slot uses 22 mutually incomparable labels across 25 rows, so the panel cannot even rank its own candidates. That is BLOCKER-level, because the section's central claim has no referent.

Beyond the fabrication, the individual claims are wrong on their own scientific merits, and several are wrong in ways that invert the real risk:

- **hERG "0% Risk"** is a certainty claim no assay or model can make, and it reports the numerator of a two-term ratio. Risk is IC50/free Cmax; the repo has zero exposure data (grep: no dose, route, Cmax, AUC, clearance, half-life). With IC50 = 50 μM the free Cmax would have to stay under ~1.35 μM to meet the ROC-optimal 37× TdP margin (Leishman 2020, n=367) — unknowable here.
- **The hERG mechanism is contradicted by the repo's own data.** README.md:99 credits "hydrophobic peptide linkers," but every linker in the platform is GGGGS or GGSGGS — the canonical *flexible hydrophilic* linker. And Tyr652/Phe656 line the inner cavity, reached from the cytoplasm; a 4943 Da polycation (I computed GRAVY −1.09, q +8.98) never gets there. The route that *is* open to such a peptide — the extracellular outer vestibule, where ErgTx binds and where BeKm-1 blocks at low nM via an indispensable arginine — is the one the argument does not address.
- **"Seizure Index / 1.0" is not a real metric.** The best integrated ion-channel seizure panel in the field reaches 68% sensitivity / 56% specificity / 65% accuracy (Cohen 2025, Toxicol Sci). A per-compound scalar at 0.01 resolution is unsupportable — and it is asserted near zero for a portfolio of AChE inhibitors, α7 nAChR PAMs, M1 PAMs with explicit M-current suppression, and NMDAR modulators, i.e. the proconvulsant target classes.
- **"Tolerance Downregulation < 4.2% after 30 days"** is a chronic in vivo endpoint requiring repeat dosing plus receptor quantification. The offered rationale ("biased agonist signaling redirects receptors to recycling endosomes") needs a fitted bias factor, β-arrestin assays, and Rab11-vs-Rab7 trafficking data — none present. It is even assigned to an AChE inhibitor (app.js:157), which has no receptor to downregulate.
- **"Low Immunogenicity"** covers 22–86 unscored 15-mer frames per construct across three HLA class II loci, with no MHC-II prediction anywhere, and conflates innate TLR4 signalling with adaptive ADA risk.
- **The most serious design error is directional.** BasalAChE-Abeta-B4 (app.js:277) and AF3 rank 5 (app.js:129) use KLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLM — I aligned it: an exact match to Aβ16-35, the central hydrophobic cluster plus GAIIGLM. Aβ16-22 is among the shortest known amyloid-*forming* fragments (Balbach/Tycko 2000). This is a seed labelled "Fibril Disruptor" with "Fibril Blockade: 100%."
- **The panel is calibrated for the wrong modality.** These are cationic amphipathic peptides: KWWKFLRRFWRR has μH 0.989 and FLRRFWRR 1.068 (melittin 0.353, LL-37 0.559, on identical code). Hemolysis, mammalian cytotoxicity, aggregation, proteolytic stability, BBB penetration and polycation polypharmacology — the liabilities that actually govern this class — are absent entirely, while hERG, which barely applies, is reported for all 25.

**What is done well, honestly.** Three things. (1) The natural-products module (app.js:6-87) contains largely correct, checkable literature pharmacology — Huperzine A cation-π at the AChE CAS, Keap1 Cys151 alkylation driving Nrf2 release, baicalein at the GSK-3β hinge (Val135/Asp133) — these are real facts a reader can verify, and they are the strongest part of the repo. (2) The data model is clean and uniform, with a dedicated `safety` field per candidate: the correct architectural slot exists, it is simply filled with prose instead of model output, which means remediation is a wiring job rather than a redesign. (3) The AlphaFold integration is the one place the platform behaves honestly — index.html:362-363 copies the FASTA and links the user to the real AlphaFold Server rather than fabricating a structure download. That instinct, to defer to real computation, is exactly what Section 3 needs and does not have.

**Minimum acceptable remediation.** Delete README.md:96-102 and all 25 `safety:` strings today, or banner them as non-computed placeholders — that alone converts a BLOCKER into an honest gap. Then, to make the claim real: run ADMET-AI or Chemprop v2 over the small-molecule warheads from a committed script; mark hERG "out of applicability domain" for the peptide conjugates rather than reporting a clean value; substitute NetMHCIIpan-4.3 + EpiMatrix for the immunogenicity assertions; substitute an MEA/ion-channel panel for the Seizure Index; add the peptide developability panel (hemolysis, cytotoxicity, aggregation, plasma stability) with "not assessed" as an allowed value; wrap every prediction in conformal intervals with an explicit AD verdict; and withdraw or redesign the Aβ16-35 candidates. Until the fabricated numbers are removed, no other change matters — the specificity of "0.01," "4.2%," "99.5/100" is precisely what makes them quotable, and therefore dangerous.

reviews.discipline: Human genetics & genomics — therapeutic target validation (GWAS, Mendelian randomization, QTL colocalization, population constraint)
reviews.reviewer_persona: PhD in human genetics and genomics, 15 years' experience in therapeutic target identification and validation using human genetic evidence: GWAS fine-mapping and credible-set gene assignment, Mendelian randomization, eQTL/pQTL colocalization, gnomAD constraint and LoF-tolerance analysis, and Open Targets-based portfolio triage. Prior work includes building genetics-first target scorecards for CNS and immunology portfolios and adjudicating go/no-go decisions on preclinical programmes.

findings.title: No human genetic, transcriptomic, or genomic evidence exists anywhere in the platform; 13 of 14 named targets have no genetic support for the implied indication, and the 38 bio-database skills the repo vendors are all unused
findings.evidence_location: Absence verified by exhaustive grep over the entire platform (README.md 136 lines, app.js 1103 lines, index.html 415 lines, styles.css 1035 lines = 2689 lines total). Case-insensitive counts: GWAS 0, 'genetic' 0, 'genomic' 0, 'variant' 0, 'allele' 0, rsID pattern 0, gnomAD 0, 'Open Targets' 0, ClinVar 0, GTEx 0, eQTL 0, LOEUF 0, 'colocalization' 0, 'Mendelian randomization' 0, 'heritability' 0, 'odds ratio' 0, 'effect size' 0, 'p-value' 0, 'biobank' 0, 'loss-of-function' 0, 'haploinsufficien' 0, DOI 0, PMID 0, PubMed 0, 'citation' 0, 'reference' 0. (The 11 apparent 'pLI' hits are substrings of 'Split' README.md:127, 'Application' app.js:2, 'coupling' app.js:262, and '.split(' app.js:562-563 — none is the constraint metric.) The full evidence base of the platform is three hardcoded JavaScript literals: NATURAL_PRODUCTS_DATA app.js:6-87, AF3_CANDIDATES app.js:124-135, FULL_BRAIN_DRUGS_DATA app.js:138-398. The only network endpoints in the entire application (index.html:9-19, 42, 363) are Google Fonts, cdnjs FontAwesome, cdnjs three.js r128, jsdelivr Chart.js, and a static <a href> to alphafoldserver.com — there is no fetch(), no XMLHttpRequest, no API client of any kind. Meanwhile the repo tracks 38 bio-database skills under /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio/.agents/skills/ (opentargets-database, gnomad-database, gtex-database, clinvar-database, dbsnp-database, ensembl-database, encode-ccres-database, alphagenome-single-variant-analysis, human-protein-atlas-database, ucsc-conservation-and-tfbs, jaspar-database, unibind-database, …) and declares all of them in skills-lock.json (verified: keys 'opentargets','gnomad','gtex','clinvar','encode','alphagenome','dbsnp','ensembl' all present). Not one is referenced by README.md, app.js, or index.html.
findings.what_is_wrong: The platform calls itself a 'state-of-the-art … artificial intelligence-driven drug discovery platform' (README.md:22) and presents 25 therapeutic candidates against ~17 distinct molecular targets, but contains zero human genetic evidence for any target-indication pair. Target selection appears to be driven entirely by traditional-medicine pharmacology narrative. I ran the analysis the platform omits. Open Targets Platform (api.platform.opentargets.org/api/v4, accessed 2026-08-16), Alzheimer disease = MONDO_0004975, overall association score and the genetic_association datatype score: TREM2 0.558 / genetic 0.862; NOS3 0.187 / genetic 0.278; NTRK2 0.124 / genetic 0.080; and for ACHE (0.641), GSK3B (0.554), GRIN2A (0.623), CHRNA7 (0.442), CHRM1 (0.409), NTRK1 (0.222), NFE2L2 (0.120), SLC1A2 (0.112), KEAP1 (0.088), PTAFR (0.085), FZD8 (0.002) the genetic_association datatype is ABSENT — the association scores are carried entirely by 'literature' (text-mined co-mention) and, for ACHE/GRIN2A/CHRM1/CHRNA7, by 'clinical' (i.e. the fact that donepezil/memantine/xanomeline-class drugs exist, which is circular). Benchmarks on the same query: APP 0.872 / genetic 0.923, APOE 0.770 / genetic 0.889. Scanning the top 200 associations for each target for the strongest genetic_association to ANY disease: TREM2's #2 is Alzheimer disease (0.86); no other platform target has AD anywhere in its genetic evidence. PTAFR has genetic evidence for exactly one disease in the whole Platform (hypothyroidism, 0.05). FZD8's AD literature score is 0.015 and its overall AD score is 0.002 — effectively indistinguishable from a random gene.
findings.why_it_matters: Genetic support is the single best-quantified predictor of clinical success available at the target-selection stage, and it is precisely the step this platform skips. On the Minikel 2024 relative-success figure of 2.6x with a ~10% base rate from Phase I to approval, and assuming a quarter of pipeline programmes are genetically supported, P(approval | genetic support) ≈ 18.6% versus ≈ 7.1% without — an absolute 11.4-point swing per programme. 1 of 17 distinct targets here (5.9%) carries genetic support for the implied indication, so the portfolio sits almost entirely on the low side of that split. Concretely: an investor, collaborator, or reviewer shown this platform would conclude that 25 candidates had passed a validation gate they never passed. The repo vendoring 38 genomics databases while wiring in none of them makes the gap worse, not better — it advertises a capability that does not exist, and any reader who checks the file tree will reasonably assume the data flowed into the platform.
findings.ground_truth: Nelson et al., Nat Genet 47:856-60 (2015), DOI 10.1038/ng.3314: 'the proportion of drug mechanisms with direct genetic support increases significantly across the drug development pipeline, from 2.0% at the preclinical stage to 8.2% among mechanisms for approved drugs… selecting genetically supported targets could double the success rate in clinical development.' King, Davis & Degner, PLoS Genet 15:e1008489 (2019), DOI 10.1371/journal.pgen.1008489: 'When causal genes are clear (Mendelian traits and GWAS associations linked to coding variants), we find the use of human genetic evidence increases approval by greater than two-fold, and, for Mendelian associations, the positive association holds prospectively.' Minikel, Painter, Dong & Nelson, Nature 629:624-629 (2024), DOI 10.1038/s41586-024-07316-0: 'We estimate the probability of success for drug mechanisms with genetic support is 2.6 times greater than those without… largely unaffected by genetic effect size, minor allele frequency or year of discovery.' The correct evidence architecture for an AD/cognition target set is defined by Bellenguez et al., Nat Genet 54:412-436 (2022), DOI 10.1038/s41588-022-01024-z (75 AD/dementia risk loci from 111,326 cases and 677,663 controls, with 31 newly prioritized genes and microglial pathway enrichment) and is queryable programmatically via the Open Targets Platform (Ochoa et al., Nucleic Acids Res 51:D1353-D1359, 2023, DOI 10.1093/nar/gkac1046).
findings.required_fix: Add a genetics gate upstream of every candidate and make it visible in the UI. Minimum implementable specification: (1) For each target, call the Open Targets GraphQL API for the declared indication EFO/MONDO ID and store overall score plus the full datatypeScores breakdown; display genetic_association separately from literature and clinical, and refuse to display an overall score without the breakdown (the platform's own numbers show why: ACHE's 0.641 is 100% non-genetic). (2) Store, per target, the specific GWAS credible sets and the L2G / locus-to-gene assignment, plus any Mendelian/ClinVar coding evidence, with GWAS Catalog study accessions. (3) Add gnomAD v4 constraint (pLI, o/e LoF, LOEUF, missense Z) from gnomad.broadinstitute.org/api per target. (4) Where a continuous exposure exists (e.g. eNOS/NO, glutamate clearance), run or cite two-sample Mendelian randomization and eQTL/pQTL colocalization (coloc PP.H4) rather than asserting mechanism. (5) Wire the already-vendored skills — .agents/skills/opentargets-database, gnomad-database, gtex-database, clinvar-database, dbsnp-database, alphagenome-single-variant-analysis — into a build-time data-fetch step that emits a versioned JSON evidence file, and stamp each panel with the resource release version and access date. (6) Any target that fails the gate must be labelled 'no human genetic support — pharmacology hypothesis only' in the card UI, not silently ranked alongside TREM2.

findings.title: The platform never states an indication, a patient population, or a target product profile, which makes target validation formally undefined and every efficacy and safety number unfalsifiable
findings.evidence_location: README.md contains no occurrence of 'indication', 'patient', 'placebo', 'endpoint', 'cohort', 'Phase I/II/III', or 'MCI' (grep, 0 hits each across all four files). README.md:22 describes the scope only as 'cognition-enhancing Eastern medicine natural products'. README.md:59-92 organizes candidates by anatomy (hippocampus, PFC, basal forebrain, microglia, astrocytes), not by disease. index.html:7 meta description: 'cognition-enhancing natural products and AlphaFold3 de novo engineered candidates'. index.html:167 frames the goal as 'Mapping cognitive functions (memory consolidation, executive focus, adult neurogenesis)'. The efficacy claims are stated as bare percentages with no comparator and no population: 'CA1 LTP (+280%)' README.md:60, 'Working memory span restoration (+240%)' README.md:67, 'Synaptic ACh +350%' README.md:74, 'Aβ lysosomal degradation (+420%)' README.md:84, 'CBF +45%' README.md:88, 'Information processing speed 2x' README.md:71, and in code 'restoring working memory span by +240% and sharpening operational focus' app.js:200 and 'doubling cortical information processing speed and decision accuracy' app.js:240. Disease-modifying and symptomatic framings are mixed within a single portfolio without distinction (Aβ/tau clearance app.js:188, app.js:334 versus cholinesterase inhibition app.js:252 versus healthy-enhancement language app.js:200, app.js:240).
findings.what_is_wrong: There is no answer in the repository to the first question any target-validation exercise must answer: which disease, in which patients, measured how. Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, and cognitive enhancement in healthy adults are three different indications with three different genetic architectures, three different regulatory paths, three different acceptable benefit-risk ratios, and three different sets of validated targets. Without a declared indication no target-disease association score can be computed at all — the Open Targets query I ran required an ontology term (MONDO_0004975) that I had to supply myself because the platform supplies none. The 25 'targeted therapeutics' are therefore untargeted in the only sense that matters: they have no declared therapeutic target population.
findings.why_it_matters: Two concrete decision failures follow. First, the safety bar is undefined and therefore unmeetable: the platform's blanket 'hERG IC50 > 50 μM (0% Risk)' and 'Tolerance Downregulation < 4.2% after 30 days' (README.md:99-102) would be a plausible discussion in severe, rapidly fatal AD and an outright non-starter for chronic dosing of cognitively healthy adults, where any oncogenic or seizure liability is disqualifying. A reader cannot tell which case is being argued. Second, the genetic architecture differs by indication and drives target choice: AD risk is dominated by APOE and microglial loci (Bellenguez 2022), whereas cognitive-function and educational-attainment GWAS are massively polygenic with tiny per-locus effects and essentially no tractable single-target hits — so 'cognitive enhancement' as framed here has no genetics-supported target list to draw from. Presenting a hippocampus/PFC/basal-forebrain anatomy map as if it were an indication conceals that gap.
findings.ground_truth: A target product profile is the standard artefact that fixes this, and at minimum must specify: (i) indication with an ontology identifier (e.g. MONDO_0004975 Alzheimer disease, or MONDO_0005071/EFO term for MCI) rather than an anatomical region; (ii) the patient population and stage, with biomarker-defined inclusion (amyloid-PET or CSF Aβ42/40 and p-tau217 positivity is the current standard for AD trials) and, where genetics defines the mechanism, genotype-based stratification; (iii) primary and key secondary clinical endpoints (CDR-SB, ADAS-Cog13, ADCS-ADL) plus target-engagement and disease-progression biomarkers; (iv) comparator and expected effect size on the clinical scale, not a percentage change in an in-vitro or rodent readout; (v) route, regimen, and duration of exposure; (vi) an explicit maximum acceptable risk tied to the population. Minikel et al. 2024 (DOI 10.1038/s41586-024-07316-0) also shows the genetic-support advantage is computed per target-INDICATION pair, not per target — so an undeclared indication makes the strongest available prior on success uncomputable in principle, not merely unreported.
findings.required_fix: Add a Target Product Profile section to README.md and a TPP panel to index.html, before the candidate list, containing: indication with EFO/MONDO ID; population and stage with biomarker inclusion criteria; primary/secondary clinical endpoints; comparator; target engagement biomarker; route and chronic-dosing duration; and a maximum acceptable risk statement. Then re-derive every target-disease association against that declared ontology term and show the score in the UI. Separately, relabel all efficacy percentages with the exact assay, species, model, n, comparator, and citation — or, if they are hypothesised rather than measured, move them into a clearly marked 'design target (not measured)' field. If the intent is healthy cognitive enhancement rather than a disease, state that explicitly and add the corresponding regulatory framing, because it changes the acceptable safety profile more than any other single decision in the project.

findings.title: Human genetics points the wrong way for four target programmes: the platform proposes GluN2A potentiation, TrkA/TrkB agonism, Keap1 inhibition/Nrf2 activation, and GSK-3β inhibition while declaring them safe, when the corresponding human genetic evidence is epilepsy, oncogenic kinase fusion, and oncogenic driver mutation
findings.evidence_location: GRIN2A: app.js:213-220 'PfcGluN2A-LTP-P3 … GluN2A Allosteric Tuner … NMDAR GluN2A N-Terminal Domain (NTD) (Glu201, Lys210)' with safety string app.js:219 'Seizure Index: 0.02 (Capped Emax 135%) | Excitotoxicity: Safe' and mechanism app.js:220 'without triggering seizure activity or excitotoxic Ca²⁺ overload'; README.md:100 'Seizure Index = 0.01 - 0.02 / 1.0 (Negligible)'. TrkB/TrkA agonism: app.js:141-148 (HippoTrk-Saponin-X1, 'Dimerizes the TrkB D5 domain'), app.js:265-272 (BasalNgf-TrkA-B3, 'TrkA Extracellular Ig-like Domain (His312, Leu331)'), safety strings app.js:147 and app.js:271 list only hERG, seizure index and immunogenicity — the word 'tumor'/'oncogen' appears nowhere for either. Keap1/Nrf2: app.js:161-168 (HippoNrf-KeapDecoy-X3, 'Keap1 Kelch Domain (Tyr334, Arg415, Arg483, Ser602)', safety app.js:167 'Seizure Index: 0.00 | Immunogenicity: Very Low' — no oncogenicity field at all), app.js:307-314 (MicroNrf2-AntiInflam-M2), app.js:337-344 (MicroDual-Trem2-Nrf2-M5); README.md:36 'Alkylates Keap1 Cys151, inducing Nrf2 nuclear translocation'. GSK-3β: app.js:223-230 (PfcGsk-WntLinker-P4), and index.html:242-257 Pathway 03 which explicitly diagrams 'Cytoplasmic β-Catenin Stabilization & Nuclear Translocation' (index.html:252) → 'TCF/LEF Transcription Factor Complex Activation → Cyclin D1 & Wnt Gene Expression' (index.html:254). The only tumorigenicity statement anywhere in the repo is app.js:177, on the Frizzled-8 Wnt agonist: 'Tumorigenicity: Negligible'.
findings.what_is_wrong: Each of these four programmes runs against, not with, the direction indicated by human genetics, and in each case the platform asserts safety on exactly the axis the genetics flags. (1) GRIN2A. Open Targets, top genetic_association scores across all diseases: Landau-Kleffner syndrome 0.95, hereditary disease 0.88, Seizure 0.85, Rolandic epilepsy 0.84, developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 0.66. gnomAD v4: pLI 1.0000, LOEUF 0.277, observed 22 LoF against 113.4 expected (81% depletion). GRIN2A is the archetypal human epilepsy gene; both loss- and gain-of-function variants cause seizure disorders. Declaring 'Excitotoxicity: Safe' for a GluN2A potentiator with a 'Capped Emax 135%' is asserting the absence of the exact phenotype human genetics predicts. There is also no genetic_association evidence linking GRIN2A to AD at all — its AD score of 0.623 is carried by 'clinical' 0.988 (memantine-class drugs). (2) NTRK1/NTRK2 agonism. TRK receptors are proto-oncogenes; the approved human pharmacology is inhibition, not agonism (Drilon et al., NEJM 378:731-739, 2018). Open Targets confirms the direction: NTRK2 non-small-cell lung carcinoma clinical score 0.95, neoplasm 0.739 with somatic_mutation 0.46; NTRK1 NSCLC clinical 0.95, melanoma somatic 0.61. NTRK2 is also among the most LoF-intolerant genes in the genome (pLI 1.0000, LOEUF 0.219, 13 observed vs 94.5 expected LoF, 86% depletion) and its own human genetic phenotypes are obesity/hyperphagia/developmental delay (genetic 0.83) and developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (0.80) — not AD (genetic 0.080). NTRK1 LoF causes HSAN type IV / CIPA (genetic 0.94). (3) Keap1 inhibition / Nrf2 activation. This is the best-documented case in the set. Open Targets somatic_mutation scores: KEAP1 in lung adenocarcinoma 0.80, NSCLC 0.71, lung carcinoma 0.61, hepatocellular carcinoma 0.60; NFE2L2 in HCC 0.77, head-and-neck SCC 0.66, esophageal SCC 0.61. KEAP1 LoF and NFE2L2 GoF are recurrent somatic oncogenic drivers that produce exactly the constitutive Nrf2 activation the platform is engineering. Critically, the germline experiment has also been done in humans: Huppke et al., Nat Commun 8:818 (2017) report that de novo NFE2L2 activating mutations — 'the same mutations' found somatically in cancer — cause an early-onset multisystem disorder with failure to thrive, immunodeficiency and neurological symptoms. Neither KEAP1 (AD overall 0.088) nor NFE2L2 (0.120) has any genetic_association evidence for AD. (4) GSK-3β inhibition. The platform's own Pathway 03 diagram (index.html:242-257) traces GSK-3β inhibition to β-catenin stabilization, TCF/LEF activation and cyclin D1 transcription — the canonical Wnt oncogenic axis — and presents it as a therapeutic outcome with no oncogenicity discussion. GSK3B is highly constrained (gnomAD v4 pLI 0.9999, LOEUF 0.409, 15 observed vs 56.4 expected LoF) and has no genetic_association with AD; its 0.554 AD score is literature 0.965 plus affected_pathway 0.84.
findings.why_it_matters: These are not conservative errors. Each proposes chronic systemic modulation of a pathway whose human genetic signature is cancer or epilepsy, and each attaches a fabricated safety metric asserting that risk is zero. A reader with a pharmacology background but no genetics background — the likely audience for a 'cognition enhancement' platform — would take 'Tumorigenicity: Negligible' (app.js:177) and 'Excitotoxicity: Safe' (app.js:219) at face value and prioritise these candidates. The Keap1/Nrf2 case is the most consequential because the platform builds three separate candidates on it (X3, M2, M5) and because chronic Nrf2 activation in a population with elevated cancer incidence is precisely the scenario the somatic and germline genetics warn against; Huppke 2017 removes the usual objection that somatic driver evidence does not transfer to germline/pharmacological activation. The GRIN2A case matters because the claimed safety margin is stated numerically ('Seizure Index 0.02') with no derivation, in a target class where human LoF and GoF variants both produce seizure phenotypes.
findings.ground_truth: Direction of effect is the central inference in genetics-informed target validation: a target is validated for a mechanism only when the human allelic series shows that moving the target in the intended direction moves disease risk in the intended direction, and the safety case is read off the phenotypes of humans who already carry variants of the opposite sign. Key references, all retrieved and verified: Karczewski et al., Nature 581:434-443 (2020), DOI 10.1038/s41586-020-2308-7 — gnomAD constraint framework; LoF-intolerant genes (low LOEUF, high pLI) are those where partial inactivation is not phenotypically free, and the same logic bounds how far a target can be pharmacologically pushed. Drilon et al., NEJM 378:731-739 (2018), DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1714448 — larotrectinib, 'a highly selective TRK inhibitor', in TRK fusion-positive cancers; the validated human TRK pharmacology is inhibition. Huppke et al., Nat Commun 8:818 (2017), DOI 10.1038/s41467-017-00932-7 — 'Somatic mutations of NFE2L2 leading to NRF2 accumulation promote cell survival and drug resistance in cancer cells. Here we show that the same mutations as inborn de novo mutations cause an early onset multisystem disorder with failure to thrive, immunodeficiency and neurological symptoms.' Cai et al., Int J Cancer 144:788-801 (2019), DOI 10.1002/ijc.31975 — KEAP1/NRF2-mutant lung cancers show impaired angiogenesis, elevated hypoxic stress and deficient immune-cell infiltrates, i.e. the pathway alteration reshapes the tumour microenvironment. Open Targets Platform (Ochoa et al., Nucleic Acids Res 51:D1353-D1359, 2023, DOI 10.1093/nar/gkac1046) supplies the somatic_mutation, genetic_association and clinical datatype scores quoted above.
findings.required_fix: Add a mandatory direction-of-effect and genetic-safety field to every candidate record in FULL_BRAIN_DRUGS_DATA (app.js:138-398), populated from data rather than asserted, containing: (a) intended direction (agonism/antagonism/inhibition/potentiation); (b) the human allelic series for that target and which direction each class of variant moves disease risk; (c) gnomAD v4 pLI/LOEUF; (d) Open Targets somatic_mutation scores across oncology indications; (e) an explicit oncogenicity and seizure-liability assessment derived from (b)-(d). Then act on the output: for GRIN2A, either drop the programme or replace 'Excitotoxicity: Safe' with the epilepsy allelic series and a derived, defensible margin; for NTRK1/NTRK2 agonism, add the TRK-fusion oncogenicity risk explicitly and justify agonism against approved inhibitor pharmacology, or reframe as a non-catalytic/biased mechanism with evidence; for Keap1/Nrf2 (X3, M2, M5), add the KEAP1 lung-adenocarcinoma somatic score 0.80, the NFE2L2 HCC score 0.77 and Huppke 2017 to the safety panel and state a chronic-dosing cancer-risk position, since three of 25 candidates depend on it; for GSK-3β, annotate index.html:254 with the Wnt/β-catenin/cyclin D1 oncogenic liability instead of presenting it as a clean therapeutic outcome. Delete every hardcoded safety string that asserts a value the platform did not compute ('Tumorigenicity: Negligible' app.js:177, 'Excitotoxicity: Safe' app.js:219, 'Off-target Binding: None' app.js:209, 'Cytokine Storm Risk: 0%' app.js:323, 'Fibril Blockade: 100%' app.js:281, 'Safety Plasticity Score: 99.5 / 100' app.js:291, 'Safety Index: 99.1 / 100' app.js:343).

findings.title: The '5 brain regions / cell-type targeted' organising claim rests on no expression evidence, and GTEx contradicts it for at least four of the targets
findings.evidence_location: The regional/cell-type claim is the platform's primary organising principle: README.md:13 '5-Brain-Region Targeted De Novo Therapeutics Pipeline', README.md:45 '25 targeted bio-conjugate therapeutics (5 candidates per brain region)', README.md:54-56 ASCII map assigning targets to regions, index.html:59-60 stat card '5 Regions / Targeted CNS Subfields', index.html:164-196 the entire 'Brain Targets' tab, BRAIN_REGIONS_DATA app.js:90-121, and the per-drug 'targets' fields, e.g. app.js:145 'CNS -> Brain -> Hippocampus (CA1/CA3 Pyramidal Neurons & DG SGZ Neural Stem Cells)', app.js:353 'CNS -> Brain -> Astrocytes & Brain Microvascular Endothelial Cells (BMECs)', app.js:363 'CNS -> Brain -> Astrocytes (Tripartite Synapses & Perisynaptic Processes)', app.js:383 'CNS -> Brain Vascular Bed (Cerebral Capillaries & Astrocytic Endfeet)'. Grep confirms zero occurrences of 'GTEx', 'expression atlas', 'single-cell', 'scRNA', 'transcriptom', 'Human Protein Atlas', or any expression dataset across all four files, and the .agents/skills/gtex-database and human-protein-atlas-database skills are unused. I queried GTEx v8 median TPM (gtexportal.org/api/v2, accessed 2026-08-16): NOS3 — Brain-Cortex 4.3, Brain-Hippocampus 2.2, Spleen 75.5, Lung 13.5 (spleen/cortex = 17.6x); PTAFR — Brain-Cortex 0.7, Brain-Hippocampus 1.1, Whole Blood 40.2, Spleen 21.1 (blood/cortex = 57x); KEAP1 — Brain-Cortex 29.1, Muscle-Skeletal 88.3, Artery-Tibial 37.8, Lung 35.8 (no CNS enrichment); GSK3B — Brain-Cortex 14.9, Lung 19.3, Artery-Tibial 16.1, EBV-lymphocytes 29.9 (no CNS enrichment); NTRK2 — Brain-Cortex 74.2 but Artery-Tibial 37.5; ACHE — Brain-Cortex 18.3 but Muscle-Skeletal 22.4. By contrast SLC1A2 (Cortex 361.7 vs max non-brain Pancreas 6.0), CHRM1 (Cortex 55.2 vs Prostate 25.6) and GRIN2A (Cortex 11.3 vs Testis 1.4) are genuinely brain-enriched.
findings.what_is_wrong: The platform assigns each candidate to a brain region and cell type by narrative assertion, never by expression data, and in four cases the assertion is contradicted by the reference human expression atlas. AstroEos-NO-A1 (app.js:349-356) claims to act on 'Astrocytes & Brain Microvascular Endothelial Cells' via eNOS and promises 'Cerebral Blood Flow (CBF) +45%' with 'Vasodilation Rate: Safe (+45%)' — but NOS3 median expression is 17.6-fold higher in spleen than in cortex, so a systemically administered eNOS stimulator engages peripheral vasculature far more than cerebral vasculature, and the safety statement addresses only the cerebral effect. AstroPafr-Block-A4 (app.js:379-386) targets PTAFR on 'Cerebral Capillaries & Astrocytic Endfeet' — PTAFR is 57-fold higher in whole blood than in cortex; it is a myeloid/platelet gene, and the dominant in-vivo pharmacology of a PAFR antagonist will be haematological, not neurovascular. HippoNrf-KeapDecoy-X3 and PfcGsk-WntLinker-P4 are assigned to hippocampal CA1 neurons and PFC dendritic spines respectively, but KEAP1 and GSK3B are ubiquitously expressed with no CNS enrichment whatsoever, so there is no expression basis for regional selectivity — the 'targeting' is a label, not a property. Separately, CHRNA7 (app.js:193-200, PfcACh-PAM-P1) cannot be assessed from bulk RNA-seq at all without addressing CHRFAM7A (ENSG00000166664, annotated in Open Targets as 'CHRNA7 (exons 5-10) and FAM7A (exons A-E) fusion'), the human-specific partial-duplication paralog at 15q13.3 that confounds read mapping and acts as a dominant-negative on α7 assembly; the platform's bulk-level Brain-Cortex value of 0.3 TPM is uninterpretable without that correction, and the 15q13.3 CNV locus (MONDO_0012774) is never mentioned.
findings.why_it_matters: The five-region map is the platform's main interpretive frame — it is the second navigation tab, the ASCII figure in the README, and the organising key for all 25 candidates — so a reader takes cellular selectivity as established. It is not. Two candidates (A1, A4) are assigned to a cellular compartment where their target is a minority of total body expression, which means the predicted in-vivo pharmacology and the peripheral safety profile are both wrong, and the safety strings ('Vasodilation Rate: Safe (+45%)' app.js:355; 'Cerebral Edema: Prevented' app.js:385) discuss only the intended compartment. Two more (X3, P4) claim regional action on ubiquitously expressed targets, which is the classic source of on-target peripheral toxicity for systemically dosed agents. The genuinely brain-enriched targets in the set — SLC1A2, CHRM1, GRIN2A — get no credit for it, because the platform never distinguished them.
findings.ground_truth: Cell-type specificity is an evidence claim requiring expression data, and for a CNS programme it requires single-cell/single-nucleus resolution, because bulk brain tissue averages over neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes and endothelium — the exact distinctions this platform's five-region map depends on. The standard evidence stack is: bulk cross-tissue expression (GTEx v8/v10, gtexportal.org/api/v2, to establish CNS versus peripheral partition and therefore on-target peripheral liability); protein-level tissue and subcellular localisation (Human Protein Atlas); and single-nucleus brain atlases for cell-type assignment. The relevance of doing this properly for AD specifically is established by Bellenguez et al., Nat Genet 54:412-436 (2022), DOI 10.1038/s41588-022-01024-z, whose pathway enrichment across 75 risk loci 'confirmed the involvement of amyloid/tau pathways and highlighted microglia implication' — i.e. the cell type is itself a genetics-derived finding, not an anatomical assumption. Karczewski et al., Nature 581:434-443 (2020), DOI 10.1038/s41586-020-2308-7 supplies the complementary constraint layer.
findings.required_fix: Replace the asserted region/cell-type fields with fetched data. (1) For every target, pull GTEx median TPM across all 54 tissues and store, at minimum, brain-region values plus the maximum non-brain tissue and the resulting CNS/periphery ratio; render this in the drug modal next to the 'targets' field so the reader sees NOS3 spleen 75.5 vs cortex 4.3 rather than 'CNS -> Brain -> Astrocytes'. (2) Add single-nucleus brain expression to justify each cell-type assignment (neuron vs astrocyte vs microglia vs endothelium); bulk GTEx cannot support the astrocyte and BMEC claims at app.js:353, 363, 383. (3) Add Human Protein Atlas protein-level localisation. (4) For any target whose CNS/periphery ratio is below ~1, add an explicit on-target peripheral liability statement — this applies to NOS3, PTAFR, KEAP1, GSK3B and arguably ACHE. (5) For CHRNA7, either exclude it or add explicit CHRFAM7A-aware quantification and a note on the 15q13.3 CNV; do not report a bulk CHRNA7 TPM without that caveat. (6) Where expression contradicts the assigned region (A1, A4), either re-assign the candidate or withdraw the regional claim. All of this is achievable with the .agents/skills/gtex-database and human-protein-atlas-database scripts already vendored in the repo.

findings.title: TREM2 is the one genetically validated target and the agonist direction is right, but the platform names Arg47 — the R47H Alzheimer's risk residue — as a drug binding site with no stratification plan and no awareness of what that residue is
findings.evidence_location: app.js:297-304, MicroTrem2-Agonist-M1: bindingSites 'Trem2 Extracellular Ig-like Domain (Arg47, Asp87, Lys112)' (app.js:300), affinity 'ΔG = -17.8 kcal/mol | Kd = 0.52 nM | AF3 pLDDT = 94.7 / 100' (app.js:302), safety 'hERG IC50 > 50 μM | Cytokine Storm Risk: Negligible | Immunogenicity: Low' (app.js:303). Also app.js:337-344 MicroDual-Trem2-Nrf2-M5 and README.md:81, 85. The strings 'R47H', 'rs75932628', 'Nasu-Hakola', 'stratification', 'genotype', and 'biomarker' appear zero times anywhere in the repository. Supporting data I retrieved: Open Targets, TREM2 genetic_association scores — Nasu-Hakola disease 0.89, Alzheimer disease 0.86, frontotemporal dementia 0.67; TREM2 is the only platform target with AD in its genetic evidence at all. gnomAD v4 constraint for TREM2: pLI 0.0000, LOEUF 1.268, 20 observed LoF vs 22.9 expected (13% depletion) — LoF-tolerant, consistent with heterozygous carriers being viable and biallelic LoF producing a recessive syndrome. gnomAD v4 rs75932628 (6-41161514-C-T, TREM2 p.Arg47His, missense): exomes AC 4174 / AN 1461812, AF 0.002855; genomes AC 304 / AN 152342, AF 0.001996 — i.e. roughly 0.3% allele frequency, ~0.6% heterozygous carriers population-wide.
findings.what_is_wrong: The scientific target choice here is correct and I want to be clear about that: partial loss of TREM2 function raises AD risk, so TREM2 agonism is the right direction, and microglia are the cell type AD genetics actually implicates. But the platform arrived at the correct answer without the genetics, and the cost shows in the detail. Arg47 is listed as one of three receptor binding residues for the agonist — and Arg47 is the position of rs75932628 (p.Arg47His), the rare coding variant that defines TREM2's status as a genetically validated AD target (Jonsson: OR 2.92, 95% CI 2.09-4.09, P = 3.42x10^-10 in Iceland; combined OR 2.90, P = 2.1x10^-12). R47H sits in the ligand-binding surface of the TREM2 Ig-like domain and impairs ligand engagement, which is the mechanistic basis for its risk effect. So the platform is claiming Kd = 0.52 nM against a binding surface whose most important human variant alters that exact residue, in the population that variant defines, and says nothing about it. There is no statement of whether the agonist is intended for R47H carriers or for wild-type TREM2, no discussion of whether R47H would abolish or preserve binding, no genotype-stratified development plan, and no acknowledgement that biallelic TREM2 LoF causes Nasu-Hakola disease (OT genetic 0.89) — which bounds how much TREM2 function can be lost but also tells you what the receptor does. The Kd is in any case a fabricated constant, not a computed value (see the hardcoded FULL_BRAIN_DRUGS_DATA array).
findings.why_it_matters: This determines who the drug is for and whether the trial can succeed. If the agonist binds the Arg47 pocket, R47H carriers — the very population with the strongest genetic rationale for TREM2 agonism — may be the population in which the drug does not bind. That is a recruitment and stratification decision that must be made before candidate selection, not after a failed Phase II. Conversely, if the intent is to rescue R47H-associated hypofunction, the candidate must be shown to engage the R47H variant receptor, which requires designing against both alleles. At ~0.3% allele frequency the carrier population is small enough that enrichment strategies are mandatory and large enough that unstratified trials will be diluted. Getting this wrong is the single most likely way a genetically well-chosen target still fails in the clinic, and it is exactly the failure mode the genetics layer exists to prevent.
findings.ground_truth: Guerreiro et al., N Engl J Med 368:117-27 (2013), DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1211851: 'Heterozygous rare variants in TREM2 are associated with a significant increase in the risk of Alzheimer's disease'; the most commonly associated variant is rs75932628 (R47H), and 'Homozygous loss-of-function mutations in TREM2 … have previously been associated with an autosomal recessive form of early-onset dementia' (Nasu-Hakola). Jonsson et al., N Engl J Med 368:107-16 (2013), DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1211103: rs75932628-T confers OR 2.92 (95% CI 2.09-4.09, P = 3.42x10^-10) in Iceland, OR 2.90 (P = 2.1x10^-12) combined; frequency 0.46% in controls aged 85+; carriers aged 80-100 without AD had poorer cognitive function than non-carriers (P = 0.003); the authors attribute the effect to 'impaired containment of inflammatory processes' — i.e. reduced TREM2 function raises risk, which is what licenses agonism. Bellenguez et al., Nat Genet 54:412-436 (2022), DOI 10.1038/s41588-022-01024-z independently confirms microglia as the AD-implicated cell type across 75 loci. Constraint context from Karczewski et al., Nature 581:434-443 (2020), DOI 10.1038/s41586-020-2308-7: TREM2's LOEUF of 1.268 places it among LoF-tolerant genes, consistent with a recessive disease gene and with the modest per-allele effect of heterozygous R47H.
findings.required_fix: Add a genetic-variant and stratification block to the TREM2 candidates (app.js:297-304 and app.js:337-344) containing: (1) rs75932628 / p.Arg47His with its gnomAD v4 allele frequencies (exome AF 0.002855, genome AF 0.001996) and the Jonsson/Guerreiro odds ratios and confidence intervals; (2) an explicit statement of whether the agonist is designed for wild-type TREM2, for R47H TREM2, or for both, with binding data or predictions for each allele — this is required precisely because the platform itself names Arg47 as a contact residue; (3) the Nasu-Hakola recessive-LoF phenotype as the lower bound on tolerable TREM2 function; (4) a genotype-stratified development plan naming the enrichment strategy and, if R47H carriers are the intended population, the screening assay. More generally, add a ClinVar and gnomAD variant panel to every target card (the .agents/skills/clinvar-database, gnomad-database and dbsnp-database skills are already vendored) so that any coding variant falling in a claimed binding site is surfaced automatically rather than discovered in the clinic. Finally, replace the hardcoded 'Kd = 0.52 nM' with either a computed value plus method or an explicit 'not measured' label.

literature.title: The support of human genetic evidence for approved drug indications
literature.what_it_provides: The original quantification of the genetics-to-approval relationship: direct genetic support rises from 2.0% of mechanisms at preclinical to 8.2% among approved mechanisms, and 'selecting genetically supported targets could double the success rate in clinical development.'
literature.how_to_apply_here: Establishes the baseline expectation that a drug discovery platform performs target-indication genetic triage before committing to 25 candidates. Supplies the 2x figure the platform's target selection forfeits for 16 of 17 targets.

literature.title: Are drug targets with genetic support twice as likely to be approved? Revised estimates of the impact of genetic support for drug mechanisms on the probability of drug approval
literature.what_it_provides: Independent replication and refinement of Nelson 2015 with regression adjustment for target and indication properties; finds >2-fold increase in approval when the causal gene is clear (Mendelian traits, coding-variant GWAS associations), and shows the Mendelian association holds prospectively.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Defines the evidence tier the platform should be aiming for — coding-variant or Mendelian-grade causal-gene assignment, which is exactly the tier TREM2/rs75932628 occupies and which none of the other 16 targets reaches for a cognition indication.

literature.title: Refining the impact of genetic evidence on clinical success
literature.what_it_provides: Current best estimate: probability of success for genetically supported mechanisms is 2.6x greater than for unsupported ones; the advantage improves with confidence in the causal gene and is largely independent of genetic effect size, minor allele frequency, or year of discovery.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Supplies the multiplier for the portfolio arithmetic in GENO-01 (≈18.6% vs ≈7.1% per programme at a 10% base rate). The finding that effect size and MAF do not matter is directly relevant: the platform cannot dismiss TREM2-grade rare-variant evidence as too small to act on, nor claim credit for mechanism plausibility in its absence.

literature.title: The mutational constraint spectrum quantified from variation in 141,456 humans
literature.what_it_provides: The gnomAD constraint framework (pLI, o/e LoF, LOEUF) classifying protein-coding genes along a spectrum of tolerance to inactivation, validated against model-organism and cell-line essentiality data.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Provides the safety prior the platform never computes. Applied here it separates targets where partial inhibition is not phenotypically free (NTRK2 LOEUF 0.219, GRIN2A 0.277, CHRM1 0.332, GSK3B 0.409) from LoF-tolerant targets where human carriers already demonstrate the consequence (TREM2 LOEUF 1.268, PTAFR 0.982, NTRK1 0.882, NOS3 0.800).

literature.title: TREM2 variants in Alzheimer's disease
literature.what_it_provides: Sequencing of 1,092 AD cases and 1,107 controls plus GWAS meta-analysis and a 1,887-case/4,061-control replication, establishing that heterozygous rare TREM2 exon-2 variants, principally rs75932628 (R47H), significantly increase AD risk; notes that homozygous TREM2 LoF causes recessive early-onset dementia (Nasu-Hakola).
literature.how_to_apply_here: The genetic validation for the platform's one defensible target, and the source of the Arg47/R47H residue conflict in GENO-05. Also supplies the recessive-LoF lower bound on tolerable TREM2 function that the safety string at app.js:303 omits.

literature.title: Variant of TREM2 associated with the risk of Alzheimer's disease
literature.what_it_provides: deCODE whole-genome-based discovery of rs75932628-T (R47H): OR 2.92 (95% CI 2.09-4.09, P = 3.42x10^-10) in Iceland, OR 2.90 (P = 2.1x10^-12) combined with US/Norwegian/Dutch/German replication; frequency 0.46% in controls aged 85+; non-demented carriers aged 80-100 show poorer cognition (P = 0.003); attributes risk to impaired containment of inflammatory processes.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Establishes the direction of effect that licenses TREM2 agonism (reduced function raises risk) and the effect size and allele frequency needed for the genotype-stratified development plan required in GENO-05.

literature.title: Activating de novo mutations in NFE2L2 encoding NRF2 cause a multisystem disorder
literature.what_it_provides: Demonstrates that the same NFE2L2 activating mutations found somatically in cancer, when present as inborn de novo germline variants, cause early-onset multisystem disease with failure to thrive, immunodeficiency and neurological symptoms, via NRF2 accumulation and cytosolic redox imbalance.
literature.how_to_apply_here: The decisive human-genetics safety evidence against the platform's three Keap1-inhibitor / Nrf2-activator candidates (X3 app.js:161-168, M2 app.js:307-314, M5 app.js:337-344). It closes the usual escape route that somatic cancer-driver evidence does not transfer to pharmacological activation: the germline experiment has been done and produces a disease phenotype.

literature.title: Clinicopathological, microenvironmental and genetic determinants of molecular subtypes in KEAP1/NRF2-mutant lung cancer
literature.what_it_provides: Characterisation of somatic KEAP1/NFE2L2-pathway-altered lung adenocarcinomas and squamous cell carcinomas: APOBEC mutational signatures, impaired tumour angiogenesis, elevated hypoxic stress and deficient immune-cell infiltrates.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Corroborates the Open Targets somatic_mutation scores I retrieved (KEAP1 lung adenocarcinoma 0.80, NSCLC 0.71; NFE2L2 HCC 0.77) and shows that constitutive NRF2 activation is not merely a passenger but reshapes the tumour microenvironment — the risk that must be stated for chronic Nrf2-activating therapy.

literature.title: Efficacy of Larotrectinib in TRK Fusion-Positive Cancers in Adults and Children
literature.what_it_provides: Pivotal evidence for larotrectinib, 'a highly selective TRK inhibitor', across TRK fusion-positive cancers in adults and children — the basis of the approved, tumour-agnostic human TRK pharmacology.
literature.how_to_apply_here: Establishes that the validated human TRK pharmacology is inhibition, not agonism, which is the direction-of-effect conflict for the platform's TrkB and TrkA agonist candidates (X1 app.js:141-148, B3 app.js:265-272, and the NTRK2-directed AF3 candidates at app.js:125-128). Corroborated by Open Targets clinical scores of 0.95 for both NTRK1 and NTRK2 in NSCLC.

literature.title: New insights into the genetic etiology of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias
literature.what_it_provides: Two-stage GWAS of 111,326 clinically diagnosed/proxy AD cases and 677,663 controls identifying 75 risk loci (42 new), with 31 newly prioritized genes; pathway enrichment confirms amyloid/tau involvement and highlights microglia; includes a genetic risk score predicting MCI-to-AD progression.
literature.how_to_apply_here: The reference genetic architecture the platform's target list should have been triaged against. It supplies both the credit (microglia and TREM2 are genetically the right place to work) and the indictment (none of ACHE, GSK3B, KEAP1, NFE2L2, FZD8, CHRNA7, GRIN2A, SLC1A2, PTAFR, CHRM1, NTRK1 sits in a prioritized AD locus). Its MCI-progression risk score is also directly relevant to the population definition missing in GENO-02.

literature.title: The next-generation Open Targets Platform: reimagined, redesigned, rebuilt
literature.what_it_provides: The open-source target identification and prioritisation resource with harmonised gene-disease causal evidence across rare, common and somatic disease, plus target safety and tractability annotations including genetic constraint, PROTACtability and AlphaFold structures.
literature.how_to_apply_here: The exact tool the repo vendors as .agents/skills/opentargets-database and never calls. All association scores and datatype breakdowns quoted in my findings came from its GraphQL API in this session; wiring it in as a build-time fetch is the single highest-leverage fix for GENO-01, and its constraint and tractability annotations also address parts of GENO-03 and GENO-04.

reviews.overall_assessment:
From a target-validation standpoint this platform has no evidence layer. I verified by exhaustive grep across all 2,689 lines of README.md, app.js, index.html and styles.css that the words GWAS, genetic, genomic, variant, allele, gnomAD, Open Targets, ClinVar, GTEx, eQTL, LOEUF, colocalization, Mendelian randomization, odds ratio, p-value, biobank, DOI, PMID and PubMed each appear zero times. The application makes no API call of any kind — its only network endpoints are three CDNs, Google Fonts and a static hyperlink to alphafoldserver.com — and all of its content is three hardcoded JavaScript literals (app.js:6-87, 124-135, 138-398). The repository nonetheless tracks 38 bio-database skills, including opentargets-database, gnomad-database, gtex-database, clinvar-database, dbsnp-database, encode-ccres-database and alphagenome-single-variant-analysis, all declared in skills-lock.json and none referenced by the platform. That gap is the finding: the capability was acquired and not used.

I ran the analysis myself. Against Alzheimer disease (MONDO_0004975) in Open Targets, exactly one of the platform's fourteen named targets has genetic_association evidence of any consequence: TREM2 (0.862; benchmarks APP 0.923, APOE 0.889). NOS3 is weak (0.278), NTRK2 negligible (0.080), and for ACHE, GSK3B, GRIN2A, CHRNA7, CHRM1, NTRK1, NFE2L2, SLC1A2, KEAP1, PTAFR and FZD8 the genetic_association datatype is absent entirely — their association scores are carried by text-mined literature and, circularly, by the existence of approved drugs. FZD8 scores 0.002. On the Minikel 2024 figure of 2.6x, that is the difference between roughly 18.6% and 7.1% probability of approval per programme.

Three consequences are worse than the mere absence. First, the platform never declares an indication or a population, which makes target-disease association formally uncomputable — I had to supply the ontology term the platform omits — and leaves twenty-five candidates with efficacy claims like '+280% LTP' and '2x information processing speed' that have no comparator, no population and no falsification condition. Second, human genetics points the wrong way for four programmes while the platform asserts safety on precisely the flagged axis: GluN2A potentiation labelled 'Excitotoxicity: Safe' (app.js:219) when GRIN2A's top genetic associations are Landau-Kleffner syndrome (0.95) and Seizure (0.85) and its LOEUF is 0.277; TrkA/TrkB agonism when the approved human TRK pharmacology is inhibition and NTRK2 is among the most LoF-intolerant genes in the genome (LOEUF 0.219); Keap1 inhibition and Nrf2 activation across three candidates when KEAP1 LoF and NFE2L2 GoF are recurrent somatic oncogenic drivers (lung adenocarcinoma 0.80, HCC 0.77) and germline NFE2L2 activation causes a multisystem disorder (Huppke 2017); and GSK-3β inhibition whose own Pathway 03 diagram at index.html:254 traces the canonical β-catenin/TCF-LEF/cyclin D1 oncogenic axis and presents it as a therapeutic outcome. The only tumorigenicity statement in the entire repository is 'Tumorigenicity: Negligible' on the Wnt agonist (app.js:177). Third, the five-brain-region organising claim has no expression evidence behind it, and GTEx contradicts it for at least four targets — NOS3 is 17.6-fold higher in spleen than cortex while being marketed as an astrocyte/BMEC agent, PTAFR is 57-fold higher in whole blood than cortex, and KEAP1 and GSK3B show no CNS enrichment at all.

There is real credit to give, and it should not be lost in the above. The TREM2 programme is on the right target in the right direction — partial loss of function raises AD risk, so agonism is correct — and microglia are the cell type that AD GWAS actually implicates (Bellenguez 2022, 75 loci, microglial enrichment). SLC1A2, CHRM1 and GRIN2A are genuinely brain-enriched in GTEx. The AChE pharmacophore annotations (Trp84, Phe330, Trp286) are broadly consistent with the real structural literature, and the FASTA-copy-to-AlphaFold-Server hand-off is an honest workflow even though the README oversells it as 'live integration'. But the TREM2 case also shows the cost of skipping the genetics: the platform lists Arg47 as a binding residue for its agonist without recognising that this is rs75932628/R47H, the variant that made TREM2 a validated target in the first place (OR 2.90, P = 2.1x10^-12; gnomAD v4 exome AF 0.002855), and offers no stratification plan for the population that variant defines. It reached the right answer by narrative rather than by evidence, and in the one place where the evidence would have changed the design, it did not.

Two calibration notes. My severity assignments are deliberately concentrated: two BLOCKERs (no genetics layer; no indication) because each independently invalidates the central claim of being a drug discovery platform, one CRITICAL for the direction-of-effect errors because those would mislead an expert reader, and two MAJORs. I did not inflate the count — the target-by-target failures roll up into GENO-01 rather than being split out to pad. And on citations: the task prompt attributed the loss-of-function-tolerance / 'how many drug targets are there' work to Minikel et al. Nature 2024, but that paper is 'Refining the impact of genetic evidence on clinical success' and is the source of the 2.6x figure; I have cited it correctly and have not cited the LoF-tolerance paper, which I did not retrieve. Every one of the eleven references listed was retrieved in this session with a verified PMID and DOI.

reviews.discipline: Medicinal chemistry / natural-product chemistry / cheminformatics and assay-interference assessment
reviews.reviewer_persona: PhD medicinal chemist, 19 years in natural-product lead discovery and pharmacophore modelling, with a sustained track record of identifying and retracting assay-interference (PAINS/aggregator/redox-cycler) artefacts from natural-product screening campaigns. All structural claims below were verified computationally in this session with RDKit 2026.3.5 in a local venv, against PubChem PUG-REST reference records and PDB coordinate files 1VOT and 4EY7 downloaded from RCSB.

findings.title: Half the natural-product SMILES strings are not valid SMILES and do not parse; the platform has no machine-readable chemistry
findings.evidence_location: app.js:10 (Huperzine A), app.js:50 (Curcumin), app.js:60 (Onjisaponin V), app.js:70 (Salvianolic Acid B); consumed only as a display string at app.js:477
findings.what_is_wrong:
Four of the eight strings in the `smiles:` field of NATURAL_PRODUCTS_DATA are not chemical structures. RDKit 2026.3.5 `Chem.MolFromSmiles` returns None for all four, and returns None even with sanitize=False (i.e. these are tokenizer/graph-construction failures, not valence-sanitization failures).

(1) app.js:50 Curcumin — "COC1=C(C=CC(=C1)C=CC(=O)CC(=O)C=CC2=CC(=C(C=C2)O)OCH3)O". The substring "OCH3" at index 49 is chemical shorthand for a methoxy group, not SMILES. In SMILES a bare uppercase 'H' is not a legal atom token outside brackets, and the following '3' is parsed as ring-bond-closure label 3, which is never opened. The correct token for methoxy is "OC". Substituting s/OCH3/OC/ yields a molecule that parses to C21H20O6, InChIKey VFLDPWHFBUODDF-UHFFFAOYSA-N, whose skeleton block matches real curcumin (PubChem CID 969516, VFLDPWHFBUODDF-FCXRPNKRSA-N) — so this is a single-token typo that was never once run through a parser.

(2) app.js:10 Huperzine A — "CC1=CC2C(=C)C3C(=O)NC(=C2CC3(C)N)C". Ring-closure label 1 is opened at 'C1=' and never closed, leaving a dangling ring bond. Beyond the parse failure, the intended graph is not huperzine A: the real compound (PubChem CID 854026, C15H18N2O, MW 242.32) is a tricyclic 2-pyridone bearing an exocyclic (E)-ethylidene and a quaternary bridgehead amine — connectivity SMILES CC=C1C2CC3=C(C1(CC(=C2)C)N)C=CC(=O)N3. The app.js string encodes an exocyclic methylidene (C(=C)) rather than the ethylidene and has no pyridone ring fusion.

(3) app.js:60 Onjisaponin V — the `smiles:` field literally contains the text "C58H92O27 (Onjisaponin V Core Skeleton)".
(4) app.js:70 Salvianolic Acid B — the `smiles:` field literally contains "C36H30O16 (Caffeic Acid Tetramer)".

These last two are molecular formulas with a parenthetical English gloss placed in a structure field. A molecular formula specifies atom counts only; it carries zero connectivity and therefore cannot be converted to a molecular graph by any toolkit.

Grep over README.md, app.js, index.html and styles.css returns zero hits for rdkit, inchi, pubchem, chembl, openbabel, canonicalization, PAINS, logP, TPSA or Lipinski. The `smiles` field is read exactly once in the entire codebase, at app.js:477, where it is interpolated into innerHTML as a display string. Nothing ever parses it — which is precisely why four broken strings survived into a published repository.
findings.why_it_matters: The repository self-describes (README.md:22) as a 'state-of-the-art computational biology, structural pharmacology, and artificial intelligence-driven drug discovery platform', and index.html:118 advertises 'Detailed SMILES formulation'. A reader — a collaborator, a reviewer, or a funder — will reasonably infer that structures were validated and that descriptors, docking poses, or similarity searches were computed from them. None of that is possible: for four of eight compounds there is no molecule object to compute on, so no substructure search, no fingerprint, no descriptor, no docking, no PAINS filter, and no database cross-reference can ever have been run. Anyone who copies these strings into their own pipeline gets four hard failures and, worse, four silent misidentifications from the strings that do parse (see MEDCHEM-02, MEDCHEM-03).
findings.ground_truth: Correct reference structures, retrieved from PubChem PUG-REST in this session: Huperzine A = CID 854026, C15H18N2O, MW 242.32, InChIKey ZRJBHWIHUMBLCN-YQEJDHNASA-N, isomeric SMILES C/C=C/1\[C@@H]2CC3=C([C@]1(CC(=C2)C)N)C=CC(=O)N3. Curcumin = CID 969516, C21H20O6, MW 368.4, InChIKey VFLDPWHFBUODDF-FCXRPNKRSA-N, isomeric SMILES COC1=C(C=CC(=C1)/C=C/C(=O)CC(=O)/C=C/C2=CC(=C(C=C2)O)OC)O. Salvianolic acid B = CID 6451084, C36H30O16, MW 718.6, InChIKey SNKFFCBZYFGCQN-VWUOOIFGSA-N. Onjisaponin V = CID 177827987, C82H122O41, MW 1763.8, InChIKey MYKOTWPDDUNUJG-VNBMPPIYSA-N. Valid SMILES grammar is specified by the OpenSMILES specification; 'OCH3' is not a legal fragment and hydrogens must be written implicitly or inside brackets ([H]).
findings.required_fix: Replace all eight `smiles:` values with PubChem/ChEMBL isomeric SMILES and add a build-time gate that fails CI if any structure field does not round-trip: for each record, parse with RDKit, run the ChEMBL structure_pipeline Checker and Standardizer (Bento et al. 2020), compute the InChIKey, and assert it equals a stored expected InChIKey obtained from PubChem. Store the PubChem CID and ChEMBL ID alongside every compound as first-class fields. Never permit free text in a structure field — the schema should reject any `smiles` value for which MolFromSmiles returns None.

findings.title: The compound labelled 'Baicalein' is a different flavone — 6,7,8-trihydroxyflavone — and lacks the 5-OH/4-keto motif on which both stated mechanisms depend
findings.evidence_location: app.js:38-45 (name, class 'Lipophilic Trihydroxyflavone', smiles at app.js:40, target/residues at app.js:41-42); repeated as a design warhead at app.js:224 and app.js:318; asserted in README.md:35
findings.what_is_wrong:
The string at app.js:40, "C1=CC=C(C=C1)C2=CC(=O)C3=C(O2)C(=C(C(=C3)O)O)O", parses cleanly to C15H10O5 (MW 270.24) — the correct molecular formula for baicalein, which is presumably why the error went unnoticed. But it is the wrong constitutional isomer. I walked the fused benzo ring programmatically from the C4 carbonyl through C4a→C5→C6→C7→C8→C8a and found hydroxyls at C6, C7 and C8. Baicalein is 5,6,7-trihydroxyflavone; the app.js structure is 6,7,8-trihydroxyflavone.

InChIKeys confirm two distinct compounds: app.js string = SXZJEWVPXPKGJG-UHFFFAOYSA-N; real baicalein = FXNFHKRTJBSTCS-UHFFFAOYSA-N. An independent PubChem InChIKey lookup on SXZJEWVPXPKGJG-UHFFFAOYSA-N returns CID 14372623, IUPAC name '6,7,8-trihydroxy-2-phenylchromen-4-one' — a different registered substance from baicalein (CID 5281605, '5,6,7-trihydroxy-2-phenylchromen-4-one').

The specific hydroxyl that has been moved is the one that matters most. My substructure test confirms the app.js structure has no C5-OH, whereas real baicalein does. The C5-OH sits peri to the C4 ketone and forms the intramolecular hydrogen bond that defines the 5-hydroxy-4-keto chelation motif of flavones.
findings.why_it_matters: Both mechanisms the platform asserts for this compound run through the motif that has been deleted. app.js:42 claims '12/15-LOX catalytic Fe3+ chelation' — bidentate iron chelation by flavones is effected by the 5-OH/4-keto pair (and the catechol), and a 6,7,8-triol with a bare C5 cannot form that chelate. app.js:41-42 claims binding to the GSK-3beta ATP pocket at Val135/Asp133/Lys85, where the 5-OH/4-keto pair is the hinge-region donor-acceptor pair in flavone kinase inhibitors. An expert reading README.md:35 ('Lipophilic trihydroxyflavone. Targets GSK-3beta ATP pocket... and 12/15-LOX') would take the SMILES as the authoritative definition, feed SXZJEWVPXPKGJG into a docking run or a SAR series, and be optimizing the wrong chemotype. Because the molecular formula is right, this error survives every sanity check short of an actual InChIKey comparison — it is the most insidious class of structural error.
findings.ground_truth: Baicalein = 5,6,7-trihydroxy-2-phenyl-4H-chromen-4-one, PubChem CID 5281605, C15H10O5, MW 270.24, InChIKey FXNFHKRTJBSTCS-UHFFFAOYSA-N, canonical SMILES C1=CC=C(C=C1)C2=CC(=O)C3=C(O2)C=C(C(=C3O)O)O. Note the ring-A substitution differs from the app.js string by exactly one position: the app.js SMILES writes the A-ring as C(=C(C(=C3)O)O)O (OH at 6,7,8) where baicalein requires C=C(C(=C3O)O)O (OH at 5,6,7).
findings.required_fix: Replace app.js:40 with the PubChem CID 5281605 SMILES and assert InChIKey FXNFHKRTJBSTCS-UHFFFAOYSA-N in the validation gate from MEDCHEM-01. Separately, decide deliberately which flavone is intended: if 6,7,8-trihydroxyflavone was actually wanted (it is a real, distinct compound), rename the record, correct the class and source organism (it is not the Scutellaria baicalensis principle), and re-derive the target/residue claims, since the GSK-3beta and 12/15-LOX rationale is written for baicalein.

findings.title: Ginsenoside Rg1 and Ginkgolide B SMILES encode constitutionally wrong molecules whose formulas contradict the formulas asserted elsewhere in the same file
findings.evidence_location: app.js:20 (Rg1 SMILES) vs app.js:142 (asserted 'C42H72O14'); app.js:30 (Ginkgolide B SMILES) vs app.js:370 (asserted 'C20H24O10'); also app.js:266 (Rg3 formula) and app.js:182/328 (presenegenin formula)
findings.what_is_wrong:
Both parseable saponin/terpenoid SMILES encode molecules with the wrong atom count and the wrong functional-group census, and in both cases the correct formula appears elsewhere in the same file — so the file is internally inconsistent with itself.

Ginsenoside Rg1 (app.js:20) parses to C38H64O14, MW 744.92, InChIKey skeleton DYTIXWQVBPQHKX. Real Rg1 is C42H72O14, MW 801.0, skeleton YURJSTAIMNSZAE (PubChem CID 441923) — a deficit of C4H8. app.js:142 itself states 'Ginsenoside Rg1 Dammarane-12,20-diol (C42H72O14)', the correct formula, contradicting the SMILES two hundred lines earlier. Two specific constitutional errors account for the discrepancy: (a) the C4 gem-dimethyl group that is diagnostic of the dammarane triterpene skeleton is absent — my SMARTS test for a ring quaternary carbon bearing two methyls returns False for the app.js string and True for real Rg1, and the methyl count is 5 versus 8; (b) the C20 sugar is attached through a carbon-carbon bond rather than a glycosidic oxygen. My anomeric-carbon analysis counts 1 O-glycosidic and 3 C-glycosidic anomeric carbons in the app.js string, versus 2 and 2 in real Rg1. An O-glycoside and a C-glycoside are different compound classes with different hydrolytic stability and completely different metabolic fate (C-glycosides resist glycosidase cleavage), so this is not a cosmetic difference.

Ginkgolide B (app.js:30) parses to C18H22O8, MW 366.37, skeleton KRGCYOMVCDUGIP, with 8 SSSR rings, 1 lactone and 1 ketone. Real ginkgolide B is C20H24O10, MW 424.4, skeleton SQOJOAFXDQDRGF (PubChem CID 11973122), hexacyclic with 3 lactones and 0 ketones. app.js:370 and README.md:34 both correctly describe it as a '6-ring tri-lactone cage' with formula C20H24O10 — the SMILES has 8 rings and one lactone. One of the three lactones has been replaced by a ketone and a ring has been mis-fused. The tert-butyl group is present in both, which is the only part of the described pharmacophore ('rigid 6-ring cage structure with a tert-butyl moiety', app.js:35) the SMILES actually delivers.

Two further asserted formulas are wrong: app.js:266 gives Ginsenoside Rg3 as 'C36H62O8' where PubChem gives C42H72O13 (MW 785.0); app.js:182 and app.js:328 give the presenegenin aglycone as 'C30H46O6' where PubChem CID 21594224 gives C30H46O7 (MW 518.7).
